text:
Michael Jones, 46, must serve 25 years for killing his son Adrian. The boy's step-mother, Heather Jones, 31, has already been jailed for the same crime.

A Kansas father has been sentenced to 25 years in prison for the killing of his seven-year-old son, Adrian Jones, a case that has shocked the state and spurred calls for stronger child protection laws. Michael Jones received the sentence after officials detailed the horrific abuse Adrian endured in the final year of his life. Heather Jones, Adrian’s stepmother, is already serving time for her role in the crime.

Adrian’s remains were discovered in November 2015 in a barn on a property rented by the Jones family. Authorities believe the boy died months earlier from starvation. Investigators initially went to the home after receiving reports of domestic abuse. While the couple awaited trial, their landlord found photos and videos on their computer that meticulously documented the abuse Adrian suffered.

During sentencing, Detective Stuart Littlefield struggled to contain his emotions as he described what he called the worst crime he had witnessed in his 23-year career. “Imagine the screams of a 7-year-old boy,” he said, recounting the abuse and its aftermath.

The case has prompted legislative action. State Representative Louis Ruiz has introduced “Adrian’s Act,” a bill that would require family members or other household residents to report suspected abuse to authorities. Under current Kansas law, only mandated reporters—such as healthcare workers, teachers, social workers, and law enforcement officers—are legally obligated to report. Adrian’s grandmother, Judy Conway, praised the proposal, saying, “If you witness child abuse, I don’t care if you’re a mandated reporter or not, we should report these things.”

Lawmakers will now consider whether to expand reporting requirements in hopes of preventing similar tragedies.

text:
A Norwich police sergeant has taken to social media to give residents a candid look at night-time policing in the city centre. Sgt Mark Shepherd, of the Norwich South Safer Neighbourhood Team, shared photographs and updates on Twitter throughout his weekend shift, highlighting the realities of late-night incidents and the importance of public engagement. Figures released by police earlier this year indicate that more than half of violent crime in Norwich occurs between 21:00 and 06:00.

Posting from after 22:00 on Saturday until after 05:00 on Sunday, Shepherd used the hashtag “#SelfiesWithCops” as he documented call-outs and offered safety messages. One tweet described “a few assaults coming in now. Also collapsed drunks,” and urged people to “#DrinkResponsibly #KnowYourLimits #AlcoholHarm Think, how will you get home?” Shepherd said the approach aims to humanise officers and build trust: “This hopefully shows we are human. People love the fact they are getting put on social media. Engagement is really important and we regularly get asked for photos. This takes it a small step further.”

The posts drew supportive responses from users, with one writing, “great sport Mark, loving the picture. You even look like you were enjoying it!” A Norfolk Police spokesperson said social media plays a positive role in policing, helping inform the public about incidents and providing another way for officers to keep in touch with residents.

text:
London Fire Brigade has urged the public to think twice before dialling 999 after a steady rise in callouts to free people stuck in everyday objects, costing taxpayers at least £377,000. The brigade says each incident costs around £290 to attend.

Crews were called to 416 incidents in 2010–11, 441 in 2011–12 and 453 in 2012–13. Firefighters say many could be avoided with greater care.

The most frequent mishaps involved handcuffs, prompting 79 callouts since 2010. Other emergencies included men with their genitals trapped in a toaster and a vacuum cleaner.

“Some of the incidents our firefighters are called out to could be prevented with a little common sense,” said Third Officer Dave Brown. “I don’t know whether it’s the Fifty Shades effect, but incidents involving items like handcuffs seem to have gone up.”

The brigade advises anyone using handcuffs to keep keys within reach and to consider alternatives before calling 999. Children were also frequent patients: 18 had heads stuck in potties or toilet seats, and 17 got fingers caught in toys, including one with a piece of Lego on his finger and another with a tambourine over his head. The service urged Londoners to use common sense, read instructions, and seek further non-emergency advice before tying up valuable 999 resources.

text:
Macedonian soldiers erected a new fence along the country’s southern border with Greece on Saturday in an effort to manage the surge of migrants moving through the Balkans, prompting clashes on the Greek side. Dozens of migrants, stranded after neighboring countries tightened entry rules, threw stones as the barrier went up. Aid groups said some 20 migrants were treated for head injuries and breathing problems. Macedonia’s interior ministry reported that 18 police officers were injured, two of whom were hospitalized.

Reports suggest Macedonian police briefly crossed into Greek territory and fired stun grenades to disperse rioters, as tensions flared near the official crossing at Idomeni. Footage from the scene showed groups chanting “Open, open” before the confrontations broke out. According to the Associated Press, roughly 250 people were involved in the clashes, with as many as 800 migrants stranded on the Greek side.

Macedonia stressed it is not closing the border entirely. A government spokesman said the newly erected fence is intended to redirect people to designated crossing points. Those crossings, however, are now limited to refugees from Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan, mirroring new restrictions imposed by Slovenia, Croatia, and Serbia. Migrants from other countries—including Iran, Morocco, and Pakistan—are being refused entry, triggering growing protests. On Thursday, hundreds of people from Morocco, Algeria, and Pakistan tore down a section of barbed wire, and others have engaged in extreme demonstrations, including sewing their mouths shut.

In a separate incident on Saturday, a Moroccan man denied entry into Macedonia suffered severe burns after climbing onto a train carriage and touching a live wire, as frustration and desperation mounted among those blocked from continuing their journey. “I have been here for 10 days with my two sons,” said Fatemeh, an Iranian woman stranded at the border. “We have decided to return to Athens and see what we will do.”

The International Organization for Migration (IOM) estimates that 105,000 migrants passed through Macedonia after arriving in Greece this month alone. From 1 January to 25 November, 721,217 migrants reached Greece, including 217,936 in October, compared with 34,442 in all of 2014. Between January and October, 388,130 Syrians arrived, and throughout 2015 close to 720,000 people—mainly from Syria, Iraq, and Afghanistan—have come to Greece, with most then moving north through Macedonia toward destinations such as Germany and Scandinavia.

A note on terminology: The BBC uses the term “migrant” to refer to all people on the move who have yet to complete the legal process of claiming asylum. This includes those fleeing conflict who are likely to be granted refugee status, as well as people seeking jobs and better lives, whom authorities may classify as economic migrants.

Former Burundian army chief Col Jean Bikomagu was gunned down as he drove through the gates of his home in Bujumbura, a family member told AFP. His daughter was badly injured in the attack. Authorities have not named suspects, but the killing adds to a wave of violence that has swept Burundi since President Pierre Nkurunziza sought and won a controversial third term.

Burundi’s 1993–2005 civil war was fought along ethnic lines, with mostly Hutu rebels battling the politically dominant Tutsi minority. Bikomagu led the Tutsi-dominated armed forces during the conflict, while Nkurunziza belonged to a Hutu rebel movement. A peace deal paved the way for Nkurunziza’s election in 2005.

His bid for a third term in July sparked months of unrest, with opposition parties and many voters calling it unconstitutional. The turmoil has forced more than 100,000 people to flee this year to neighboring countries.

text:
The waterway was completely restored by volunteers after falling into decline and was officially reopened by the Queen on 8 August 1990. It was originally opened in 1810, but gradually fell into decline after the Great Western Railway was built. Volunteers will re-enact the reopening at the Caen Hill lock flight, which is a Scheduled Ancient Monument later. The 87-mile waterway links the River Thames at Reading to the River Avon in Bath. The last time the complete length was navigable, before it was restored, was in 1950, when a stoppage at Burghfield near Reading made the canal impassable. Major structures along its route also include the Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts and Bruce Tunnel. Richard Parry, chief executive of the Canal and River Trust, said: "It's all down to the volunteers and the incredible amount of work they did that [the canal] is here. "The Kennet and Avon Canal really does enrich the lives of everyone around it, and this is a great opportunity to celebrate it and the achievement of those who restored it." Rob Dean, chairman of the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust, said: "Restoration of the Kennet and Avon has proved a huge success for our community. "The volunteers who led the restoration from the 50s to the 90s have given us a great legacy which we're pleased to help care for and improve." The success of the canal restoration spurred on the other restorations across the country.

Volunteers are set to re-enact the 1990 reopening of the Kennet and Avon Canal at the Caen Hill lock flight, marking a milestone for a waterway that was brought back from decline through decades of community effort.

First opened in 1810, the 87-mile canal links the River Thames at Reading with the River Avon in Bath. Its fortunes waned after the advent of the Great Western Railway, and by 1950 a stoppage at Burghfield near Reading had rendered the full length impassable. A volunteer-led restoration followed, culminating in a ceremony on 8 August 1990 when the Queen reopened the route.

“It’s all down to the volunteers and the incredible amount of work they did that [the canal] is here,” said Richard Parry, chief executive of the Canal and River Trust. “The Kennet and Avon Canal really does enrich the lives of everyone around it, and this is a great opportunity to celebrate it and the achievement of those who restored it.”

Rob Dean, chairman of the Kennet and Avon Canal Trust, added: “Restoration of the Kennet and Avon has proved a huge success for our community. The volunteers who led the restoration from the 50s to the 90s have given us a great legacy which we’re pleased to help care for and improve.”

Major landmarks along the route include the Dundas and Avoncliff aqueducts and the Bruce Tunnel. The canal’s revival is credited with inspiring further restoration projects across the country.

text:
Think Like a Man Too tops slow box office as Jersey Boys underwhelms; Maleficent crosses $500m worldwide

Kevin Hart’s Las Vegas ensemble comedy Think Like a Man Too led a sluggish North American box office, debuting with an estimated $30 million (£17.6m) and narrowly edging 22 Jump Street, which collected $29 million (£17m) in its second weekend. The modest frame saw holdovers dominate as audiences split among sequels and summer tentpoles.

DreamWorks Animation’s How to Train Your Dragon 2 slipped to third with $25.3 million (£14.8m), ensuring the weekend’s top three titles were all sequels. Despite a mere 22% rating on Rotten Tomatoes, Think Like a Man Too drew loyal fans, proving critical pans could not dent its appeal.

“This success is all about Kevin Hart,” said Paul Dergarabedian, senior analyst at box-office tracker Rentrak. “He’s a bona fide movie star. He’s versatile, he’s so well liked and he’s super funny. Talking about what actors are bankable and consistent, he’s right there in that group.” The comedian has now headlined three films this year to open north of $25 million, following January’s Ride Along and February’s About Last Night.

Clint Eastwood’s Jersey Boys, a screen adaptation of the Tony Award-winning musical about Frankie Valli and the Four Seasons, opened to a muted $13.5 million (£7.9m). Featuring a largely unfamiliar cast aside from Christopher Walken, the film earned mixed reviews and a 55% Rotten Tomatoes score. Time’s Richard Corliss called it “a turgid botch,” while USA Today’s Claudia Puig wrote that what was “blandly charming on stage” feels “contrived, cheesy and cliched” on screen.

Nearly three-quarters of Jersey Boys’ opening audience was over the age of 50, a demographic that tends to avoid opening-weekend rushes, giving the studio hope for steadier play in coming weeks. The stage show, which won the Tony for best musical in 2006 and has played across the globe including London’s West End, remains a potent brand with older moviegoers.

Rounding out the top five, Angelina Jolie’s live-action fairy tale Maleficent continued its robust international run, surpassing $500 million (£293m) worldwide. That makes it Jolie’s highest-grossing live-action film to date on an unadjusted basis, eclipsing her previous mark with 2005’s Mr. & Mrs. Smith, which finished with $478.2 million.

Overall, the frame reflected a slower summer corridor, with studios eyeing upcoming releases to re-energize the market and broaden appeal well beyond sequel-driven fare. Family fare remained a steady draw.

A Welsh farmer has warned of the severe distress livestock suffer when chased by dogs, likening it to “running after a heavily pregnant woman with a motor car.” Gareth Wyn Jones, of Llanfairfechan, issued the stark comparison as new figures show more than 300 dogs have been shot by landowners in England and Wales over the past five years. The data was obtained through a Freedom of Information request by the BBC.

Under current law, farmers are permitted to shoot dogs that pose an immediate threat to animals, but they must notify police within 48 hours. Jones told BBC 5 Live that public awareness remains dangerously low about the risks of walking dogs near livestock, especially during vulnerable periods such as lambing. “I don’t think farmers take it lightly on shooting people’s dogs. It has to come to the final straw,” he said.

Jones recounted a personal incident in which repeated lamb losses led him to take action. “I’ve had to do it and it’s not a nice situation to be in. We’d lost a few lambs night after night and this dog was getting let out of the house very early in the morning.”

Calling for greater responsibility, Jones said owners must keep dogs under control at all times. “[Dogs] are natural born killers. That’s what their jobs are; they are to herd or to hunt. People must understand that it’s their responsibility to take control, put their dogs on the lead, not leave them out at all times. We’ve got to drum this into them.”

text:
Farrell fires Saracens past Leicester as Tuilagi limps off in bruising Premiership clash

Saracens edged a gripping encounter at Welford Road, defeating Leicester Tigers 16-12 in a match defined by ferocious defenses, costly missed kicks and high-profile injuries watched closely by England head coach Eddie Jones. Owen Farrell was the difference, trading first-half penalties with Tigers fly-half Owen Williams before adding a third after the break and then scoring and converting the game’s only try to secure a vital away win.

With the sides locked at 6-6 at halftime, the opening period offered little daylight between two of the Premiership’s heavyweights. Farrell and Williams were flawless from the tee early on, capitalizing on infringements in a tense, tactical battle. The match’s tone shifted when Manu Tuilagi, recalled to England’s training camp only a day earlier, was forced off with an apparent right knee injury after landing awkwardly in a tackle, curtailing his comeback to a brief cameo and prompting concern for both club and country.

Saracens suffered their own setback when winger Chris Ashton, making his first start in 15 weeks following suspension for biting, departed after a clash of heads with Leicester center Jack Roberts. Yet the visitors struck decisively soon after. A loose pass from Ben Youngs was mishandled by Williams, allowing Brad Barritt to pounce before Farrell threw a deft dummy and accelerated clear to finish under the posts, adding the conversion for a seven-point swing.

Leicester remained in the hunt and ultimately claimed a losing bonus point thanks to Williams’ two second-half penalties, but pressure in the closing stages went unrewarded. Two missed kicks from Williams proved pivotal as Saracens absorbed late Tigers attacks and closed out the result to move within a single point of leaders Wasps at the top of the Premiership table.

Despite the defeat—only their second in 15 home games across all competitions—Leicester took heart from a powerful forward display. Director of rugby Richard Cockerill praised his pack and defensive effort, insisting the performance offered belief for the run-in. “It was tight, we played very well, they played well. We defended outstandingly well and our set-piece was dominant,” he said. “Saracens’ pack don’t get dominated very often but we dominated their pack today. Our boys were fantastic. There are a lot of positives. I know we are five points from the top four but we were playing the best side in Europe last season. If we can play like that away we will win more than we lose and we will keep in the mix.”

Saracens director of rugby Mark McCall admitted it was far from a complete performance but lauded his side’s resolve. “We are chuffed to bits to come here and win where they have not lost this season,” he said. “Not everything in our game was perfect, far from it. But what was tremendous was the fight we had and the effort we showed all the way through the game. We had to win without a platform because our scrum today was poor. To get a result without a scrum is tough.”

Referee: JP Doyle. For the latest rugby union news follow @bbcrugbyunion on Twitter.

text:
Gir Sanctuary’s Most Photographed Lion, Ram, Dies at 15

Ram, one of Gir Sanctuary’s most iconic Asiatic lions, died on Saturday at approximately 15 years of age, officials in Gujarat confirmed. Forest staff described him as “beautiful” and “flamboyant,” and many regarded him as the reserve’s “most photographed lion,” a testament to his striking presence and long reign over the forest.

Deputy Conservator of Forests Ram Ratan Nala told the BBC that a post-mortem was conducted to determine the cause of death. “He died from natural causes. He was cremated in the presence of government and local village officials,” Nala said. The loss resonated across nearby communities, where Ram was beloved. According to Nala, many forest staff members fasted for a day in mourning.

Gir Sanctuary, in western Gujarat, is the world’s only habitat for Asiatic lions and now supports a population of more than 500. Ram and his brother Shyam formed a dominant coalition that ruled parts of Gir for years, fathering numerous cubs and building a large pride. “Ram along with his brother Shyam ruled over Gir for many years and the two fathered many cubs over the years,” said Sandeep Kumar, Nala’s predecessor. “At one point, the duo had about two dozen cubs in their pride.”

The forest staff named the brothers Ram and Shyam—popular Indian names and also the title of a hit Bollywood film—reflecting their cultural resonance. Kumar noted the difference between lions and tigers in territorial behavior: while male tigers are solitary and defend territories alone, male lions often form coalitions, typically with a relative, to jointly protect their range.

“But every kingdom must come to an end,” Kumar added. With Ram gone and Shyam aging, the coalition’s hold is likely to weaken, opening the territory to younger male lions. For those who knew him, Ram’s death marks the close of a memorable chapter in Gir’s conservation story.

Meyer’s remarks were made while encouraging potential backers to invest $500,000 (£386,500) through the EB-5 immigrant investor program, which offers a pathway to a U.S. green card for foreign nationals whose investment helps create jobs. The EB-5 program is popular among wealthy Chinese investors, but it has long faced criticism as a vehicle for cheap financing for property developers and for potential abuses that exploit immigration incentives.

The episode comes amid broader scrutiny of the company’s business dealings. In March, Kushner Companies ended talks with Chinese conglomerate Anbang Insurance over a proposed major redevelopment in New York City, a potential agreement that had raised conflict-of-interest concerns. Jared Kushner, a senior adviser to President Donald Trump, has said he stepped away from the operations of his family’s business. text:
Fastest of his era: England great Frank ‘Typhoon’ Tyson dies

Frank “Typhoon” Tyson, the Lancashire-born fast bowler celebrated for his blistering pace and decisive role in England’s Ashes triumph of 1954-55, has died. Though his Test career spanned less than five years, Tyson left an indelible mark: in 17 Tests he captured 76 wickets at a remarkable average of 18.56.

Tyson shone brightest during England’s 1954-55 Ashes series in Australia. Selected ahead of fellow quick Fred Trueman, he took 28 wickets across five Tests, including an electrifying 7-27 in the second innings at Melbourne. In the annals of Ashes bowling performances, that haul has only been surpassed by two England greats: spinner Jim Laker, with match figures of 9-37 and 10-53 at Old Trafford in 1956, and paceman Stuart Broad, whose 8-15 at Trent Bridge ranks among the most devastating spells.

After retiring at the age of 30, Tyson had amassed 767 first-class wickets. He later emigrated to Australia, where he forged a successful second act as a coach, commentator, and writer, shaping generations of cricketers and enriching the game’s narrative with insight and authority.

Despite injuries and a relatively brief international career, Tyson was widely hailed as the fastest bowler of his era by Australian legends Sir Donald Bradman and Richie Benaud, as well as his great rival Trueman. Former Australia batsman Dean Jones wrote: “Sad to hear that Frank Tyson has passed away. Ex Vic coach. I was his student for a few of his books. Terrific cricketer. Terrific bloke.”

text:
David Gauke, the Financial Secretary to the Treasury, signalled a saver-focused approach to pension reform, saying a review of pension taxation would keep savers firmly in mind. “We need to ensure it is effective in terms of encouraging saving, and it is going in the right place,” he told BBC2’s Daily Politics Show. The TUC itself acknowledges uncertainty, but contends it is “not contentious to project a material further downward impact on living standards following Brexit.” The overall takeaway: if you accept forecasts of slower economic growth after leaving the EU, it is consistent to expect lower average earnings—though the specific figure of £38 a week should be treated as indicative rather than definitive.

The amended rule comes into effect at the end of 2020

World Rugby has approved a significant reform to international eligibility, extending the residency qualification period for players from 36 to 60 months. The change, ratified at the governing body’s council meeting in Kyoto, Japan, is designed to ensure that players have a genuine, close, credible and established link with the nation they represent.

“This is an historic moment for the sport,” said World Rugby vice-chairman Agustin Pichot. “National team representation is the reward for devoting your career, your rugby life, to your nation and these amendments will ensure that the international arena is full of players devoted to their nation, who got there on merit.” World Rugby chairman Bill Beaumont described the reform as “an important and necessary step to protecting the integrity and credibility of international rugby.”

Raising the residency period to five years is widely viewed as a measure that could help protect smaller unions, particularly the Pacific Island nations, by discouraging players from switching allegiance after relatively short stints overseas. The issue has been thrown into sharp relief by recent selections: last autumn, England capped Fiji-born Nathan Hughes and Semesa Rokoduguni after both qualified on the three-year residency rule. England head coach Eddie Jones has also included Sale’s Auckland-born Denny Solomona in his training squad, with the former rugby league winger set to become eligible for England in August under the existing regulations.

Some nations have already taken unilateral steps to limit reliance on foreign-born players. France has declared it will only select players who hold a French passport, a move intended to reinforce the national team’s identity and reduce dependence on overseas talent.

The Kyoto meeting delivered further governance changes. Argentina and Japan, reflecting their growing influence and contributions to the global game, have been granted expanded voting rights and will now hold three votes each on the World Rugby Council with immediate effect. In addition, French Rugby Federation president Bernard Laporte has been elected to the World Rugby Executive Committee.

Reaction within the sport has acknowledged both the practicality and the principle behind the residency reform. Former England and British and Irish Lions centre Jeremy Guscott said the practice of recruiting “project players” to qualify on residency “hasn’t been particularly in the spirit of rugby,” while noting that unions were operating within the laws. He suggested the longer qualification could stem the flow of Pacific Island and South African players moving abroad, or at least encourage earlier commitments, and hoped it would strengthen domestic competitions. “It is a long time for someone to commit to a new country and perform well enough over that time to make an international squad so I think five years is fair,” Guscott added.

The amended rule will take effect at the end of 2020, giving unions, players and pathways time to adjust to a landscape that places national connection at the heart of international selection.

Attempting to recover, he lost control and spun soon after rejoining, erasing any immediate hope of salvaging his earlier progress.

What followed was the day’s most compelling on-track duel, a hard-fought, wheel-to-wheel scrap with McLaren’s Jenson Button over 13th place. Maldonado initially gained the upper hand through sharp race craft and brave positioning. But the battle ended abruptly when Button missed his braking point at Turn One and collected both cars, eliminating them from contention. As is often the case with Maldonado, the incidents triggered a torrent of criticism online. Yet the question persists: is Maldonado really as bad as his reputation suggests? His raw pace has never been in doubt. The problem, as it always has been, is consistency and a tendency to crash. If any season captured Maldonado’s yin and yang, it was 2012: flashes of brilliance offset by costly errors.

The latest approach, made by one of Trew’s advisers, “came out of the blue”, according to BBC Radio Nottingham’s Notts County correspondent Colin Slater.

Trew, who met prospective buyers from the United States and China in March, has yet to conclude a deal. Slater said Hardy has not responded to the fresh overtures and is expected first to seek clarity on Notts County’s current financial position.

Trew acquired the club from Peter Trembling in 2010, taking on more than £1.5m in debt accrued during five turbulent months under the Middle Eastern consortium Munto Finance. While the club’s off-field future remains uncertain, on the pitch Notts County sit 12th in League Two, one point outside the play-off places.

Hardy was at Meadow Lane on Saturday to watch Notts draw with Crewe, while Trew was away on other business. Any agreement would end a protracted sale process and could provide stability ahead of the season’s run-in, though significant due diligence is expected before talks progress.

“I have tried in vain to work my way through the trauma that the doctors who saved my life warned me I would experience,” he wrote. “They recommended complete rest and the type of post-traumatic counselling which is available in cases like mine but I’m afraid I believed (wrongly) that making music and getting out there to perform for the audiences that bring me such joy would be therapy enough in itself.”

The nine cancelled shows were scheduled in Perth, Adelaide, Sydney, Melbourne, Brisbane and the Hunter Valley. Michael noted he has “enjoyed” recent performances across Europe but admitted he “seriously underestimated how difficult this year would be.”

Symphonica resumed this autumn after the tour was halted in November last year, just hours before a planned Vienna performance, when Michael became ill. He had completed 46 of the original 65 dates before contracting pneumonia. The singer said he would focus on recovery after his UK commitments, thanking fans for their understanding as he prioritises his health.

Man in Northern Ireland seriously ill with infection linked to heart surgery equipment; Belfast Trust warns 2,000 patients

A man in Northern Ireland is seriously ill in hospital with a rare bacterial infection linked to medical equipment used during open-heart surgery, his family has revealed. The patient underwent heart surgery in 2014 and several months later developed symptoms associated with mycobacterium chimaera, becoming increasingly unwell. In January, doctors confirmed the infection, which is now the subject of a UK-wide investigation.

His case is one of 28 known across the UK, according to the family, who said he was told he was the 27th person to be diagnosed. Fifteen people have died in connection with the infection. The family has asked for their identity to be protected but said they want the public to understand the seriousness of the illness.

On Monday, the Belfast Health and Social Care Trust wrote to around 2,000 patients who have had open-heart surgery since 2013, advising them of a potential—but low—risk. However, the family said they were shocked to read a report on the BBC News website stating that no cases had been identified in Northern Ireland. That report followed a briefing from the Belfast Trust in which it said it was not aware of any cases having presented locally.

It has since emerged that the man is being treated in Northern Ireland, raising questions about communication around the issue. The UK-wide investigation is examining links between mycobacterium chimaera and medical equipment used during cardiac procedures, with health authorities advising patients to be aware of symptoms and seek medical advice if concerned.

text:
Qatari poet Mohammed al-Ajami has had his prison sentence reduced to 15 years, his lawyer said, as the country’s Supreme Court prepares to deliver a final ruling within the next 30 days. Al-Ajami, also known as Mohammed Ibn al-Dheeb, was convicted over poems deemed critical of Qatar’s leadership and broader authoritarianism in the Arab world, in a case that has drawn sustained condemnation from human rights groups.

Advocacy organizations say al-Ajami’s trial was marred by irregularities, including court sessions held in secret, and argue his conviction violates international standards for freedom of expression. The case initially centered on a poem he wrote in 2010 that criticized the then-emir, Sheikh Hamad al-Thani. Activists, however, contend the authorities were particularly angered by a separate piece, Tunisian Jasmine, which al-Ajami recited and posted online in January 2011 at the height of regional uprisings.

In that poem, he voiced solidarity with Tunisia’s revolution, declaring, “We are all Tunisia in the face of the repressive elite,” and denounced “all Arab governments” as “indiscriminate thieves.” The verses resonated widely online as protests swept parts of the Middle East and North Africa, even as Qatar itself avoided the large-scale unrest seen elsewhere.

Al-Ajami, a father of four, has acknowledged writing the poems but maintains they were neither offensive nor seditious. He has argued that the 2010 recital criticizing the emir took place privately at his home, challenging the basis for charges of incitement. As he was led from a recent hearing, he shouted, “There is no law for this,” according to Reuters.

Freedom of expression is tightly controlled in Qatar, where political dissent is limited and defamation of the emir is criminalized. The country’s human rights record has long drawn scrutiny from international campaigners and remains a sensitive issue in its relations with the United States, which maintains a major military presence in the Gulf state. The looming Supreme Court decision will be closely watched by activists and diplomats alike.

text:
From April 2018, the total amount of dividends that company directors and shareholders can receive tax-free will fall from £5,000 to £2,000.

Chancellor Philip Hammond has confirmed the reduction in the dividend allowance as part of his Budget, describing it as a move to “address the unfairness” created by what he called “an extremely generous tax break for investors with substantial share portfolios.” The measure is the Budget’s largest single revenue-raiser and is forecast to bring in an increasing amount for the Treasury, reaching £930m in 2021-22.

The £5,000 dividend allowance was announced by former chancellor George Osborne in 2015. Mr Hammond said around half of those affected by the cut are directors and shareholders of private companies. Many small traders have structured their businesses as limited companies and remunerate themselves through a combination of salary and dividends, a strategy that will now carry a higher tax cost.

From April 2018, a basic-rate taxpayer receiving £5,000 in dividends will pay an additional £225 in tax compared with the current rules. A higher-rate taxpayer in the same position will pay an extra £975. The government argues the change will reduce incentives for individuals to incorporate for tax reasons, bringing the treatment of earned income and investment income closer into line.

Business groups warned the move could dampen investment and growth among smaller firms. Mike Cherry, national chairman of the Federation of Small Businesses (FSB), said: “Many of our members, including those on modest incomes, will now see a significant rise in their tax liabilities. FSB is concerned about the increased uncertainty this may cause across the business community. We would now like clarity over how this fits in to the publication of the government’s Business Tax Roadmap, which prioritised the importance of creating a stable and certain tax environment for small firms.” The FSB labelled the cut “a further disincentive for businesses to invest and grow.”

Self-employed representatives also voiced concern. Chris Bryce, chief executive of IPSE, which represents self-employed workers, said: “The reduction in dividend tax allowance, whether you work as a sole trader or through a limited company [will mean] you will be facing higher bills. The chancellor shouldn’t forget that growth in self-employment has driven our labour market in recent years and punitive rises in tax will make many people have second thoughts about striking out on their own.”

The change will also affect savers with significant shareholdings held outside Individual Savings Accounts (ISAs). According to the Treasury, savers account for around half of the 2.2 million people impacted by the cut, and will lose an average of about £320 a year. Among those affected, 1.4 million basic-rate taxpayers will lose an average £200, 725,000 higher-rate taxpayers will lose £440 on average, and 124,000 additional-rate taxpayers will lose about £890.

Experts said some investors can mitigate the impact by making greater use of tax-efficient wrappers. “Investors should make the most of their ISA and pension allowances, to protect as much of their wealth as possible from the taxman,” said Laith Khalaf, senior analyst at Hargreaves Lansdown.

Cleaner cleared of attempted murder after hammer attack ruled self-defence

A Glasgow High Court jury has cleared a Clydebank woman of attempting to murder a pensioner after accepting she struck him with a hammer in self-defence during a confrontation at his flat.

Gillian Lavery, 43, was found not guilty after jurors deliberated for just half an hour over the incident on 16 February 2016 at the home of Tom Winter. The court heard Ms Lavery had been cleaning Mr Winter’s flat and had known him for several years.

During the trial, the jury was told that Ms Lavery and Mr Winter had previously had a sexual relationship, with Mr Winter saying they had been intimate three or four times. He told the court he believed Ms Lavery was visiting that day for sex, but claimed he told her to leave when she said she was expecting a friend. Mr Winter said he walked out ahead of her when he was suddenly attacked from behind and repeatedly struck with a hammer.

Photographs shown to the court depicted the OAP with bruising to his head, face, arms and legs following the incident.

Under cross-examination, Mr Winter admitted he had also been expecting a “mystery woman” to arrive that day. He told the jury: “Gillian said she was bringing someone up… if the mystery woman did not turn up, I would have sex with Gillian with her consent.”

Ms Lavery gave a different account of events, telling the court she had agreed to visit because a woman called Sarah was due to come to Mr Winter’s flat and she could help make the visitor “feel comfortable.” She said tensions rose when the woman failed to appear, and that Mr Winter became angry and demanded sex, telling her: “I have already taken my tablet… his Viagra,” and, “You are not going anywhere. She is not here, so you are doing it.”

Ms Lavery said she attempted to flee but was struck with a walking stick. She told the court a hammer fell from a table during the struggle and that she used it to “get him off me” before managing to escape.

The jury accepted Ms Lavery’s assertion that she acted in self-defence and returned a not guilty verdict on the charge of attempted murder. No further charges were brought.

The case highlighted conflicting accounts about the nature of the pair’s relationship and the events leading up to the altercation, but jurors concluded the force used by Ms Lavery was a response to a perceived imminent threat. Neither party gave statements outside court following the verdict.

Net income rose to $5.43bn (Â£3.76bn) in the three months to the end of December against $4.93bn a year earlier. The bank cut costs by 7.4% to $14.26bn in the quarter. Legal expenses fell by almost 50% to $644m from $1.1bn. Salaries fell 2.4% to $6.69bn as the bank shed around 7,000 staff to 234,598, from 241,359 a year earlier.

JPMorgan Chase reported a rise in fourth-quarter profit as aggressive cost-cutting and sharply lower legal bills offset a challenging operating environment marked by pressure from falling oil prices and concerns about slowing growth in China. Net income increased to $5.43bn in the three months to 31 December from $4.93bn a year earlier, while total net revenue edged up about 1% to $23.75bn, topping analysts’ expectations.

“We had a good quarter as 2015 came to a close,” chief executive Jamie Dimon said in a statement. “The businesses generated strong loan growth and credit quality, except for some stress in energy. The consumer business continues to gather deposits, outpacing the industry,” he added. “Markets were somewhat quieter, and we saw the impact reflected in the results of our trading and asset management businesses.”

Noninterest expenses fell 7.4% to $14.26bn, helped by a near-halving of legal costs to $644m from $1.1bn, and a 2.4% decline in salaries to $6.69bn as headcount dropped by about 7,000 to 234,598. Provisions for credit losses rose 49% to $1.25bn, reflecting strains tied to the energy sector.

By business line, profit from investment banking surged 80% to $1.75bn even as revenue declined 4%, while the consumer banking unit reported a 10% rise in profit to $2.41bn. US banks broadly have faced a difficult year amid weak credit markets that discouraged risk-taking, while ongoing legal charges and higher capital requirements continued to weigh on costs.

JPMorgan is the first of the major US banks to report fourth-quarter earnings. Citigroup and Wells Fargo are due to report on Friday.

Police granted more time to question suspect as body of Sian O’Callaghan found; search for second body continues

Magistrates sitting in Swindon have granted Wiltshire Police an extension to continue questioning a 47-year-old man arrested in connection with the disappearance and death of Sian O’Callaghan. The extension allows officers to hold the suspect until early on Monday morning. The man, named locally as taxi driver Christopher Halliwell, was detained at an Asda supermarket in Swindon’s Orbital Centre on Thursday and remains in custody at Gablecross Police Station.

Miss O’Callaghan, 22, from Swindon, was last seen leaving the Suju nightclub at 02:52 GMT on Saturday, 19 March, intending to walk the half-mile back to the flat she shared with her boyfriend in Westmorland Road. A signal from her mobile phone was later picked up near Savernake Forest, and her boyfriend sent her a text at 03:24 GMT that night. Following the arrest on 24 March, police said the suspect took detectives, including Det Supt Steve Fulcher of Wiltshire Police, to a site near White Horse Hill, Uffington in Oxfordshire, about 15 miles (24km) from Swindon, where a body believed to be Miss O’Callaghan’s was discovered in a shallow grave.

A simple blood test already used to diagnose heart attacks could help identify people at risk long before they develop symptoms, researchers say. Scientists from the Universities of Edinburgh and Glasgow report that measuring troponin—a protein released when heart muscle is damaged—may offer a more precise way to assess heart risk than relying on blood pressure and cholesterol levels alone.

The study, funded by the British Heart Foundation and published in the Journal of the American College of Cardiology, followed 3,300 men with high cholesterol but no history of heart disease. Researchers found that men with higher troponin levels were significantly more likely to have a heart attack or die from heart disease over the next 15 years. Crucially, those identified as high risk and treated with preventive therapy, such as statins, not only reduced their risk but also saw their troponin levels fall.

“Troponin is almost like a barometer of heart health. If it creeps up, that’s bad and your risk of heart problems increases. If it goes down, that’s good,” said Professor David Newby, one of the study’s authors. “It also appears to predict who benefits from statins and opens a door to a whole new way of testing.” He added that troponin could complement established measures like blood pressure, cholesterol, and smoking status to build a more comprehensive risk profile.

Professor Nicholas Mills, who led the research, said the approach could help uncover “silent” heart disease in people who appear healthy. “Troponin testing will help doctors to identify apparently healthy individuals who have silent heart disease so we can target preventive treatments to those who are likely to benefit most,” he said.

Troponin tests are widely used in hospitals to confirm recent heart attacks in both men and women. The researchers believe the same test can be applied in routine risk assessments to prevent such events, although their current findings are based on men. They plan further research to confirm that the strategy is effective in women as well.

Dr Tim Chico, a cardiologist at the University of Sheffield, welcomed the findings but stressed that prevention remains paramount. “The problem with heart disease is that it remains very difficult to detect the early signs in people without symptoms, so these findings may provide a way to help identify people at risk,” he said. “Nevertheless, the best way to treat heart disease is to prevent it in the first place, and this is why a healthy diet, regular physical activity, not smoking, and maintaining a healthy weight and blood pressure is so important.”

As Christianity spread, the Church sought to recast Lupercalia into a Christian observance, aligning it with the commemoration of St Valentine. Over time, his name became synonymous with expressing love.

Today, the holiday is embraced in diverse ways around the world—through intimate dinners, public proposals, charitable acts, and digital declarations of affection. Archaeopteryx had pennaceous (quill-like) feathers all over its body, not only its wings, a new fossil - only the 11th of the creature found - reveals. These "trousers" were probably used for display, say scientists from Germany, writing in Nature journal. Their discovery adds weight to the theory that feathers originally evolved for purposes other than flight.

Archaeopteryx caused a major stir when the first fossil was unearthed in Germany in 1861 - just two years after Charles Darwin published On The Origin of Species. With the claws and teeth of a dinosaur, but the feathers of a bird, it was clearly a transitional form - apparent proof of Darwin's theory. Its German name "Urvogel" means "first bird". And though earlier bird-like dinosaurs have been unearthed since, many scientists still believe Archaeopteryx was the first capable of "flight" as we know it today.

The 11th fossil specimen was announced in 2011 and is remarkably well preserved, with detailed impressions of feathers all over its skeleton. The feathers are long and symmetrical on its upper leg and shorter lower down. Previous specimens had shown some evidence of feathered hind legs but this "completes the picture", according to Dr Oliver Rauhut and colleagues at the Bavarian State Collection for Palaeontology and Geology. These "trousers", as he describes them, may have been used for display, camouflage, insulation, brooding and manoeuvring while on the ground.

They were not primarily designed for flight but might have helped steady the bird during landing, similar to the hindlimb feathers of hawks, eagles and other modern raptors. The wing feathers of the new specimen show robust shafts - further evidence that the "first bird" really could fly. Recent studies assuming limited flight ability in Archaeopteryx "might be in error owing to the poorer preservation quality of the feathers," said Dr Rauhut. "I'm pretty sure it could fly. Though of course there is still a debate about how well it could fly," he told BBC News.

The trousers are also a new clue to the mystery of how flight evolved in modern birds. Traditionally it was thought that feathers and flight evolved hand in hand. But the wide variation of plumages in early birds and feathered dinosaurs suggests that feathers first arose for a different purpose, said Dr Rauhut. "Given the great diversity of pennaceous feathers found within different body regions and across the phylogeny, it seems plausible that the evolution of this feather type (especially in the wing, hindlimbs and tail) was primarily driven by display functions," he wrote in Nature. Only later were these feathers recruited for flight - which may have arisen many times in parallel in different feathered species, he said.

The new Archaeopteryx fossil underscores the complex, multifaceted journey from dinosaur to bird, reinforcing the view that modern birds are the living legacy of their dinosaur ancestors and that the origins of flight were likely as diverse as the feathers themselves.

The luge, which translates as 'sled', sees competitors travelling feet-first down an icy track at up to 85mph — with only a helmet for protection. The high-speed winter sport marries nerve with finesse as athletes lie supine on a streamlined pod and navigate twisting, banked ice tracks by the smallest of movements.

The luge sled is a moulded fibreglass pod shaped to the rider’s contours. It sits atop two metal runners, known as steels, which curve upward at the tips and connect to front-mounted “kufens” used to steer. Doubles sleds feature longer steels and kufens to accommodate two athletes. There are no brakes. To scrub speed, a slider must drag their feet along the ice while applying subtle pressure to the kufens — a skill that requires both precision and poise.

Despite its intimidating image, luge offers a host of physical benefits. The confined cockpit rewards fine motor control, building agility, balance and coordination through minute weight shifts. As speeds rise and G-forces build, strength and conditioning become essential to withstand the demands of the sport.

For aspiring British sliders, a first step now exists closer to home. Manchester’s Chill Factor-e hosts a dedicated 60-metre luge facility, far removed from the Olympic experience but ideal for beginners to sample the sensation. Progression beyond that introduction, however, generally means travelling abroad to access full-length tracks and coaching. Britain’s most recent Olympic luger, AJ Rosen, was born in the United States and continues to train there.

Luge traces its roots to early sledding contests in Scandinavia and the birth of skeleton and bobsleigh in Switzerland, particularly around St Moritz. According to Team GB, an Australian student, George Robertson, won what is reputed to be the world’s first international sled race in 1883 on a four-kilometre stretch of Swiss road, signalling the sport’s competitive potential.

The sport made its Olympic debut in 1964, when East Germany’s Thomas Kohler claimed the first gold medal. While equipment and venues have evolved, the Olympic programme has remained largely unchanged, and modern luge now runs on the same courses as bobsleigh.

While the FIA is pushing to bring the halo in next season, formal approval is still pending and several leading figures, including Red Bull team principal Christian Horner, have questioned the timing and design.

FIA F1 director Charlie Whiting has told teams in technical meetings to expect the halo to be mandated in 2017, prompting constructors to design their new cars to accommodate it. However, the device must clear a three-stage approval pathway: first through the strategy group comprising leading teams, the FIA and F1 commercial boss Bernie Ecclestone; then the F1 Commission, which includes all teams, sponsors, circuits, tyre suppliers, plus the FIA and Ecclestone; and finally the FIA World Council.

Sources have told BBC Sport that, alongside Horner, Ecclestone, Mercedes team principal Toto Wolff and Williams deputy team principal Claire Williams harbour reservations about the halo, which is intended to protect drivers from impacts with large flying objects. Horner said: “I am not a big fan of the halo and the limitations it has. It is an inelegant solution to the problem it is trying to deal with. I would prefer there to be more research time taken to do the job properly rather than rushing something through that may have other consequences. I certainly wouldn’t vote in favour of it.”

Vettel, a director of the Grand Prix Drivers’ Association, which broadly supports increased head protection and wants a solution deployed as soon as possible, ran the device for a single lap and reported mixed impressions. “Forward visibility was fine,” the four-time world champion said. “But it was quite a bit on top of you, (even if) you are not looking at the sky all the time. It needs some further running. I know the decision is up fairly soon. I don’t know what the results are on the actual research. UK Nuclear Lab to Turn Sellafield Plutonium into Long-Life Space Batteries for ESA

The initiative, which could generate new skilled jobs and significant multi-million-pound export revenues, aims to establish a European source of Radioactive Power Sources (RPS) for long-duration missions.

ESA funded a £1 million pilot project in 2009 to assess the cost and practicality of securing an indigenous supply of material for RPS. These ultra-long-life batteries do not propel spacecraft; rather, they provide reliable electrical power to scientific instruments far from the Sun or in harsh environments where solar energy is insufficient, underpinning ESA’s deep space exploration plans.

“We’re more than half way through the £1m pilot proving the viability of being able to extract the isotope from the civil plutonium stockpiles,” said Tim Tinsley, programme manager for NNL. “We have a quantity of this plutonium at our labs at the Sellafield site and a team of highly experienced chemists are ‘proving’ the chemical flow-sheet for the process.”

ESA’s current RPSs rely on plutonium-238, available only from Russia and the United States and largely produced in military reactors. Global supplies are constrained and could run short around 2018, threatening future missions. The isotope targeted at Sellafield—americium-241—can be extracted from aged civil plutonium and offers a more accessible, Europe-based alternative. If successful, it could support ESA projects and open an export market to countries currently dependent on plutonium-238.

“Technically, there are no barriers to the success of the project; it would be down to funding and politics within Europe and they are already tightly constrained,” Tinsley said. “ESA needs this fuel source for their space road-map—they cannot do it without it and we at NNL are doing everything we can to make that a success.”

Beyond space, americium-241 batteries could power devices in remote or inaccessible locations on Earth, such as deep-sea sensors or instruments installed deep underground in oil wells, where maintenance is impractical and a 20- to 30-year power supply is required.

ESA is expected to decide in November whether to continue funding. If ratified, NNL anticipates a steady ramp-up of jobs from 2014, leading to full-scale production around 2020, positioning the UK as a key supplier in a strategically important high-technology niche.

Philosophy-style classroom discussions are giving a measurable lift to pupils’ attainment, particularly for those from disadvantaged backgrounds, according to a large trial across 48 UK primary schools. More than 3,000 children in Years 4 and 5 (aged nine and ten) took part in hour-long Philosophy for Children (P4C) sessions and, on average, made two months’ additional progress in reading and maths over the course of a year compared with peers not on the programme. For disadvantaged pupils, gains were even greater and extended to writing.

The study, commissioned by the Education Endowment Foundation (EEF) and conducted by researchers at Durham University’s School of Education, examined whether structured dialogue that encourages questioning, reasoning and argument-building could translate into improved academic outcomes. Among pupils eligible for free school meals, reading scores improved by an average of four months, maths by three months and writing by two months.

Lead researcher Professor Stephen Gorard said the results indicate that philosophy sessions can positively influence core attainment and appear to be especially effective for those facing the greatest barriers. He added that robust evidence of what works is vital to help headteachers make the best use of pupil premium funding, which is intended to raise the achievement of children from lower-income families.

The findings are significant because many interventions designed to help disadvantaged pupils catch up often benefit their better-off peers even more, making it harder to close the attainment gap. In contrast, P4C appears to deliver a stronger impact for pupils from poorer backgrounds, potentially helping to narrow disparities.

At an estimated cost of around £30 per pupil, the programme could offer schools a cost-effective way to deploy limited resources, the report suggests. Beyond test scores, teachers involved in the trial also reported gains in pupils’ confidence, patience and self-esteem, as well as improvements in classroom talk and listening skills.

A typical P4C lesson sees pupils and teachers sit in a circle to explore a stimulus—such as a short video or a newspaper article—that raises a big idea or ethical dilemma. After a brief period of silent reflection, children discuss their questions in pairs or small groups before returning to a whole-class dialogue. Topics can be challenging and thought-provoking; for example, whether a healthy heart should be donated to someone who has not looked after their own health.

Petition to Cancel Trump State Visit Tops One Million: How UK State Visits Work and Past Controversies

More than a million people have signed a petition calling for US President Donald Trump’s proposed state visit to the United Kingdom to be cancelled, underscoring public unease over extending the highest level of diplomatic hospitality so early in his presidency. No date has been set for the visit, which was announced during Prime Minister Theresa May’s trip to Washington last week. Asked why an invitation was issued so soon after Mr Trump took office, a spokesperson for Mrs May said there is no set timeframe for when a president may be offered a state visit.

State visits are the most formal category of international visits to the UK, typically limited to two per year. They are designed to cement strategic relationships and showcase Britain’s ties with key partners. Guests receive full ceremonial honours: a formal welcome with a guard of honour, carriage procession, and a state banquet hosted by the Queen at Buckingham Palace or Windsor Castle. The programme usually includes meetings with the prime minister and other senior officials, cultural engagements, and visits to national institutions. While the Queen formally issues the invitation, the decision is taken on the advice of the government, with the Foreign Office and No 10 weighing diplomatic, economic and security considerations.

Public discontent around controversial guests is not new. In recent years, protesters have focused on leaders from countries criticised for human rights abuses. Despite outcry, past visits have gone ahead.

In October 2015, President Xi Jinping’s state visit prompted demonstrations over China’s human rights record and its rule in Tibet. Campaigners accused authorities of harassing, imprisoning and torturing activists and their families, and rights groups cited persecution for religious beliefs, discrimination against ethnic minorities, tight media restrictions, limited access to foreign publications and broadcasts, and use of the death penalty. Critics also linked UK steel job losses to Chinese steel being sold cheaply on global markets.

In October 2007, Saudi Arabia’s King Abdullah was greeted by protesters condemning the kingdom’s human rights record and urging the reopening of a corruption inquiry into a major arms deal. Demonstrators shouted “shame on you” as the royal procession passed along The Mall.

In November 2005, Chinese President Hu Jintao’s visit drew protests over human rights, Taiwan, and Tibet, including booing during events at Guildhall. Two years earlier, in November 2003, an estimated 100,000 people marched in London against President George W. Bush’s visit, opposing the US-led war in Iraq; an effigy of Mr Bush was toppled in Trafalgar Square.

Earlier decades brought their own controversies: in October 1971, veterans and former prisoners of war protested Emperor Hirohito of Japan over wartime atrocities; and among other contentious guests were Romania’s Nicolae Ceaușescu (1978), Zimbabwe’s Robert Mugabe (1994), and Egypt’s Hosni Mubarak (1991). Despite protests, successive governments have maintained that state visits serve the national interest.

Born in 1917 in New York state to an Italian-immigrant father, Zamperini discovered distance running as a boy and rose quickly through the ranks at his high school and the University of Southern California. Eventually captured by a Japanese patrol, Zamperini spent two harrowing years in prison camps. He was singled out by a brutal guard he came to call “The Bird,” and endured “constant beatings, punishments and torture, especially when bombers came over.” He refused to broadcast propaganda messages in exchange for better conditions, even as the U.S. military declared him killed in action.

After the war, Zamperini returned home, married, and became a devout Christian following an encounter with evangelist Billy Graham. Britain’s Kyle Edmund continued his impressive run with a straight-sets victory over American Ernesto Escobedo, winning 7-5 6-4 6-4 to reach the last 32. The 21-year-old Yorkshireman, ranked 84th in the world, backed up his first-round upset of 13th seed Richard Gasquet and will face American 20th seed John Isner next.

In humid, energy-sapping conditions, both Edmund and world No. 201 Escobedo struggled to find their first serves, producing a contest packed with long, bruising rallies. Edmund absorbed early pressure to edge the opening set and, despite letting six break points slip by in the second, stayed composed. Some brilliant defense earned him a seventh opportunity, prompting Escobedo to smash his racquet, and Edmund converted to establish a two-set lead after around 90 minutes.

The third set brought more resistance from Escobedo, with Edmund denied repeatedly on break points. It was the Briton’s sixth chance of the set—and 16th of the match—when he finally made the breakthrough, before confidently serving out to seal a deserved win.

“I’m very pleased, a lot of good things today,” Edmund told Eurosport. “I thought I played a much cleaner match, a lot of things went better for me against Gasquet. This was about toughing out more longer rallies, I made a few more errors, but you can’t be too tough on yourself. I thought every set I stayed tough, and when it counted towards the end I got the break.”

Meanwhile, Briton Johanna Konta overcame Bulgaria’s Tsvetana Pironkova 6-2 5-7 6-2 to move into the third round. Compatriots Andy Murray, Dan Evans and Naomi Broady are scheduled to play their second-round matches on Thursday, as British interest remains strong heading into the latter stages.

text:
Scottish new car registrations fell 17.5% in April as buyers rushed to beat new VED rules

New car sales in Scotland dropped sharply in April, with registrations down 17.5% year-on-year to 12,059, according to the Society of Motor Manufacturers and Traders (SMMT). The slide mirrors a broader cooling across the UK, where April sales were off by nearly 20% compared with the same month last year, following a record-breaking March. Industry leaders say the decline was anticipated as consumers accelerated purchases to avoid higher Vehicle Excise Duty (VED) rates that came into force on 1 April.

Under the new regime, all newly registered cars—apart from those with zero emissions—are subject to an annual flat rate charge, replacing the previous system that was more closely tied to carbon dioxide output. The change prompted a surge of registrations in March as buyers sought to minimize future tax liabilities, leaving a void in April. Despite last month’s fall, Scottish sales remain resilient, up around 1% over the first four months of the year compared with 2016.

Performance varied widely by region. Dumfries and Galloway was the worst affected area, with registrations plunging by more than 42% year-on-year in April, highlighting the uneven impact of shifting consumer sentiment and tax policy across local markets.

Scottish Motor Trade Association (SMTA) chief executive Sandy Burgess said: “With the strong March and the added incentive of beating the new rules on Vehicle Excise Duty coming into play on 1 April there was always going to be something of an ‘emergency stop’ in the results. The tail-off was evident across our dealers showrooms and even online inquiry levels have softened.”

He added that speculation over a potential scrappage scheme for older, less efficient diesel cars may have contributed to a “double whammy” in demand. “Ironically of course an introduction of such a scheme may well serve to bring a degree of ignition to the new car market,” Burgess said.

Looking ahead, Burgess noted retailers hold “fantastic levels of outstanding pre-owned vehicles” and reported a reassuring “business as usual” message for motorists considering a change, as the market adjusts to the new VED landscape.

Kerry Boyd, 20, has left her role as Kent Youth Commissioner after pausing public engagements in June while reports of a relationship were investigated. Boyd, who took a gap year from her education and business studies to serve full-time from 2014, was appointed by Kent’s police and crime commissioner (PCC) Ann Barnes in March, succeeding Paris Brown, who resigned following controversy over past Twitter posts.

A spokeswoman for PCC Ann Barnes said there were no plans to replace Boyd at present, adding that Mrs Barnes is “still thinking about ways to engage with young people.” The youth commissioner post, created by Mrs Barnes, is not a statutory role and many other counties do not have youth commissioners.

In a blog post, Mrs Barnes praised Boyd’s contribution and character: “I hope that Kerry has enjoyed her time with us – there have been tough times, certainly, but 20-year-old Kerry has risen to the challenge and we shall miss her dry sense of humour and quick wit. She has been a great advocate for my office and given up numerous evenings and weekends as she has travelled far and wide to get the widest views possible.”

Boyd, a former London 2012 Olympic Torch-bearer from Margate, paused public duties in June after reports surfaced of a relationship with former county councillor and youth leader Robert Burgess, who is believed to have acted as a referee for the £15,000-a-year role. Burgess told BBC Radio Kent at the time that he and Boyd had been “good friends.”

The PCC’s office said it will continue to explore alternative routes to ensure young people’s voices are heard across Kent, despite the decision not to immediately appoint a successor.

text:
Paul Hill, 42, has been jailed for six months at the High Court in Edinburgh for recklessly discharging a firearm and failing to appear for trial after a 1996 incident outside a pub in Killin, Perthshire. Hill, who had fled Scotland and spent years living in England, Ireland and the Channel Islands, surrendered to authorities last year, bringing an end to nearly three decades evading arrest.

The court heard that the incident unfolded after Hill spent an evening with his parents, sister and a friend at the Falls of Dochart Inn in Killin. An altercation began between Hill’s father and another man, and a witness, Crichton Davies, told Hill to go home. Davies described Hill as “really wound up.” A struggle ensued during which Hill produced a small handgun and fired a shot into the air. As Davies tried to wrest the weapon from his grasp, Hill fired a second shot upwards. The firearm was never recovered.

Hill handed himself in to police the day after the shooting and was initially charged with attempted murder. He was released on bail but failed to appear for trial in February 1997 and subsequently fled, remaining at large for many years before turning himself in last year. He admitted struggling with Mr Davies and recklessly discharging the gun, as well as failing to attend court and absconding to avoid detection and arrest.

Defence counsel Brian McConnachie QC told the court the shooting was “a one-off, impetuous, reckless act which had never been repeated.” He said that, shortly before Hill’s original trial date, the Dunblane school massacre had occurred, in which gunman Thomas Hamilton murdered 16 children and a teacher before killing himself. McConnachie said Hill’s former solicitor “somewhat unwisely” suggested Hill could be made an example of because of the prevailing climate following Dunblane, contributing to his decision to flee.

Sentencing Hill, Judge Lord Ericht acknowledged the offence of conviction was “much less serious” than the original charge but stressed the gravity of firing a weapon in public. “Nonetheless, the discharge of a firearm is a serious matter,” he said. “You have also defied the authority of the court by failing to attend for trial and evaded arrest since then.”

Hill, of Killin, Perthshire, will serve six months in prison for the offences arising from the 1996 incident and his prolonged failure to face justice.

text:
Ethiopia’s Oromia Ruling Party Drops Addis Ababa Expansion Plan After Protests and Deadly Clashes

Demonstrations by members of Ethiopia’s Oromo community have prompted the ruling party in the Oromia region to drop a controversial “master plan” to expand Addis Ababa into surrounding areas. Human rights groups, including Human Rights Watch, estimate that at least 140 people were killed by security forces during the protests, which began in November and intensified amid fears that Oromo farmers could be displaced. The government disputes the death toll, calling it an overestimate. Abiy Berhane of Ethiopia’s London embassy told the BBC that authorities had tried to avoid confrontation and that the protests were hijacked by people intent on provoking violence.

The Oromo People’s Democratic Organisation (OPDO) decided to abandon the plan after three days of discussions with local communities, state broadcaster EBC reported. OPDO, together with the Addis Ababa city authority, would have overseen implementation. Officials had maintained that the plan would be carried out only after broad consensus following in-depth consultations. However, a leading online campaigner said on Facebook that Oromo activists have dismissed the reversal as too little, too late, reflecting deep mistrust after months of unrest and reported crackdowns.

The master plan was designed to integrate areas adjacent to the capital into Addis Ababa’s rapidly expanding economy, but it triggered strong resistance in Oromia, Ethiopia’s largest region, which completely surrounds the city. Anger over the capital’s proposed expansion dates back to 2014 and builds on long-standing complaints among the Oromo that they have been excluded from political and economic power. At the 2007 census, the Oromo were Ethiopia’s largest ethnic group, with about 25 million people out of a total population of nearly 74 million.

Observers say the decision to halt the plan may ease immediate tensions, but they also note calls for independent investigations into protest-related deaths and detentions. Activists continue to demand accountability and broader reforms, while the government says it remains committed to consultation on any future development initiatives.

text:
Joseph Mathunjwa, president of the Association of Mineworkers and Construction Union (AMCU), says the union has accepted a wage deal that would end a five-month strike across South Africa’s platinum belt, with members to return Wednesday.

The stoppage, which began on 23 January when more than 70,000 workers downed tools to demand higher pay and benefits, has disrupted about 45% of global platinum supply and contributed to South Africa’s first-quarter economic contraction. Anglo American Platinum, Impala Platinum and Lonmin have not commented. Management is due to meet AMCU on Tuesday, when the deal is expected to be signed.

Addressing a stadium packed with workers who have gone unpaid for five months, Mathunjwa said the companies had "agreed to the bulk of our demands," prompting chants of "sign, sign, sign" from the crowd. The agreement is expected to lift entry-level pay toward 12,500 rand (£694) per month over the next three years, with increases varying by seniority.

The companies have reported combined lost earnings of 23.8bn rand (£1.3bn; $2.2bn) during the strike, which has sharply curtailed production in the world’s top exporter of platinum. South Africa holds around 80% of known global reserves of the metal, widely used in catalytic converters to reduce automotive emissions.

Despite the prolonged disruption, stockpiles have largely kept markets supplied. The South African rand strengthened almost 1% to 10.5575 per US dollar, its firmest level since 9 June, as investors welcomed signs of a resolution that could restore output and ease pressure on the economy.

text:
Horatio Chapple, 17, from Salisbury, was on an adventure holiday in August 2011 with the British Schools Exploring Society (BSES) when he died. The court was told the pain suffered by the bear would have influenced its behaviour and increased its stress.

An inquest has heard harrowing details of the polar bear attack that killed Eton schoolboy Horatio Chapple during a British Schools Exploring Society expedition in the Norwegian Arctic territory of Svalbard. Chapple, 17, was asleep in his tent when a polar bear entered the camp, dragged him from the tent, and inflicted fatal injuries to his head and upper body. Four others were seriously hurt before the animal was shot dead by one of the group leaders.

The injured included expedition leaders Michael Reid, 29, from Plymouth, and Andrew Ruck, 27, from Brighton and now living in Edinburgh, as well as trip members Patrick Flinders, 17, from Jersey, and Scott Bennell-Smith, 16, from Cornwall. The attack occurred in the early hours, when the group was camped on a glacier, and has prompted sustained scrutiny of expedition safety protocols in polar bear habitats.

Evidence presented to the court detailed the bear’s poor condition. A post-mortem examination found worn-down teeth, a cavity, swollen and reddened gums, and periodontitis affecting several teeth. Tests estimated the bear’s age at around 24, with experts noting that the fatality rate for Svalbard polar bears is high after 15 years, very high after 20 years, and that it is rare for a polar bear to reach 25. An independent report prepared by High Court judge Sir David Steel for BSES concluded the animal was “seriously underweight,” weighing about 250 kg (551 lbs) compared with a typical 400 kg (882 lbs). The court was told the pain and stress caused by the bear’s dental disease likely influenced its behaviour.

Sir David’s report criticised the expedition’s reliance on a tripwire alarm system to warn of a bear’s presence and recommended that a dedicated “bear watch” become standard practice for expeditions in Svalbard. It also called for a rigorous upgrade of rifle training.

BSES executive director Lieutenant General Peter Pearson, from Chepstow, Monmouthshire, said the organisation had adopted all the report’s recommendations. He noted that polar bear-specific measures had not been implemented because BSES has not returned to areas occupied by polar bears since the 2011 attack. Pearson defended the competence of the expedition leaders, Mr Ruck and Mr Reid.

The inquest continues.

title: She tumbled backwards over her cape as she sang Living For Love, her new single.

Madonna suffered a dramatic tumble during a live performance of her new single, Living For Love, after a dancer in goat horns tugged at her ruby-lined cape. Video and photos show the 56-year-old star falling backwards and landing with a loud thwack, prompting a brief, stunned silence in the venue, according to Newsbeat reporters positioned metres away. She quickly recovered, though momentarily tangled in the cloak, and pushed through to finish the song.

The slip was instantly the talk of Twitter, with “Madonna” and #shefellover trending worldwide. Fans shared concern and praise for her professionalism in carrying on. Later, Madonna reassured followers on Instagram: “My beautiful cape was tied too tight! But nothing can stop me and love really lifted me up! Thanks for your good wishes! I’m fine!”

There is a clear pause in the vocals during the fall, underscoring that she was singing live. For updates and behind-the-scenes coverage, follow @BBCNewsbeat on Twitter, BBCNewsbeat on Instagram, and Radio1Newsbeat on YouTube.

text:
Cardiff gears up for world football’s biggest club game as Champions League final heads to Principality Stadium on 3 June

Cardiff will host world football’s biggest club game on 3 June, when the UEFA Champions League final comes to the Principality Stadium, and Wales’s first minister Carwyn Jones says preparations, while challenging, are progressing well. Speaking to BBC Wales, Mr Jones called the occasion “a great showcase for Wales,” adding that authorities are working intensively to ensure the city is ready for the influx of supporters.

Thousands of fans are expected to pour into the Welsh capital for the final, which follows closely on the women’s UEFA Champions League final at Cardiff City Stadium on 1 June. The 100-day countdown to the women’s showpiece was marked on Tuesday with a choir flash mob in central Cardiff, where the trophy was unveiled to kick off celebrations.

Mr Jones said the scale and unpredictability of the men’s final add complexity to planning. “This is the biggest [event Cardiff has hosted] to my mind, no question about that,” he said. “It’s the sheer numbers of people, the sheer size of the event and the fact that we don’t know who’s going to be in the final so we don’t know where the fans are going to come from.”

Welsh international Gareth Bale starred in last year’s decider, helping Real Madrid defeat city rivals Atlético at Milan’s San Siro, but the first minister noted that this year’s finalists remain unknown. He said planners are liaising with all relevant authorities and organisations to deliver a safe, seamless experience. “Cardiff is the smallest city to have hosted the event. It’s always challenging, of course, but we’ll get there and we’ll be offering a fantastic welcome to all who come to our capital city,” he added.
