Noel Thomas, from Gaerwen, on Anglesey, is among those joining forces against their former employer.

Anglesey county councillor Noel Thomas, a former sub-postmaster, is joining a group of ex-Post Office workers preparing legal action over alleged faults in the Horizon computer system. Thomas was jailed for nine months in 2006 after admitting false accounting totalling £48,000. He maintains he was driven to falsify records after experiencing unexplained discrepancies, claiming a glitch in Horizon added thousands of non-existent pounds to his accounts. The Post Office has denied his claim.

Tens of other sub-postmasters have reported similar issues, alleging money disappeared from branch accounts due to software faults in Horizon, which records transactions at hundreds of Post Offices and sub-Post Offices across the UK. They say there is no alternative but to begin civil proceedings to uncover the cause of the discrepancies and seek redress.

Earlier this year, the BBC’s Panorama programme alleged the existence of a document suggesting the Post Office did not believe Thomas was guilty of theft. Thomas said he hopes that document will be made public during the civil action. A Post Office spokesperson said the organisation had not been informed of any impending court case. Previously, the Post Office stated it could not comment on individual cases due to confidentiality, and that financial loss combined with false accounting is often sufficient evidence to support a theft charge.

High Cross House in Dartington, Devon, will close to the public after the National Trust activated a pull-out clause in its lease, citing insufficient visitor numbers to make the site financially sustainable. The charity took on a 10-year lease in January 2012, but the landmark attracted 21,000 visitors in its first year—11,000 fewer than the 32,000 the Trust says were needed to break even. Dartington Hall Trust, the property’s owner, said there are no current plans to reopen the house for now. The decision effectively ends the National Trust’s management of the property.

“Whilst it is disappointing that High Cross House is now closing to the public, we continue to welcome people to the Dartington Hall Estate,” said Vaughan Lindsay, chief executive of Dartington Hall Trust. He added the owner is still exploring options for the building’s future use.

Designed in 1932 by Swiss-American architect William Lescaze, High Cross House is widely regarded as one of the UK’s finest examples of modernist architecture.

Massaro and Willstrop reach World Series Finals after late-night semis

Massaro, the defending champion, booked her place in Saturday’s World Series Finals title match after a late-night victory over Egypt’s Nouran Gohar, prevailing 12-14, 12-10, 11-7. The 33-year-old Briton will face Egyptian world number one Nour El Sherbini after a schedule pushed deep into the night because of Ramadan.

“It’s a tough situation for us both,” Massaro said of the midnight finish. “It’s really late and even though you get up late and do everything you can to recover, your body clock says that you should be in bed and not warming up for a squash match.”

In the men’s draw, world number six James Willstrop upset top-ranked Karim Abdel Gawad of Egypt 14-12, 11-6 to reach his first World Series Finals championship match in a 17-year professional career. He will meet Egypt’s Mohamed El Shorbagy in Saturday’s final.

“I’m 33, I’ve had time out like a few of us have, but I’m not taking it for granted that I’ll be able to get back to where I was when I was 29, it’s not that simple,” said the Yorkshireman.

The World Series Finals serve as the season-ending championship for both the men’s and women’s professional tours.

The pair captured Olympic gold in the men’s synchronised 3m springboard in Rio, before Laugher added a silver in the individual 3m springboard six days later. Their honours cap a breakthrough year for British diving.

Paralympic rower Laurence Whiteley is also appointed MBE for services to rowing after winning gold in the mixed trunk and arm double sculls with teammate Lauren Rowles in Rio. Samantha Barks Lands Éponine in Les Misérables Film After Surprise Onstage Announcement

Samantha Barks has been cast as Éponine in the forthcoming film adaptation of Les Misérables, following a surprise announcement delivered onstage at Manchester’s Palace Theatre. Moments after Barks finished performing as Nancy in Oliver!, producer Cameron Mackintosh appeared before the curtain to reveal that the 21-year-old Isle of Man native will join a star-studded cast that includes Hugh Jackman and Russell Crowe.

Describing the news as the “happiest moment,” Barks said it was “still sinking in” and “the biggest surprise of my life.” Mackintosh, who previously cast Barks as Éponine in a theatre production of the musical, told the audience he had searched in Hollywood, on New York’s Broadway and across London’s West End to find the right actress. He added that director Tom Hooper had chosen Barks to reprise the role on the big screen.

The announcement comes after reports that singer Taylor Swift was in line to play the tragic Éponine, one of the central characters in Victor Hugo’s 19th-century tale of love, loss and revolution in France. The film, slated for a December release, will also feature Anne Hathaway and Amanda Seyfried, the latter known for her role in the film version of Mamma Mia!

Mackintosh hailed Barks’s ascent as “so rare” in the industry. “This is a real rags-to-riches story — a 17-year-old who had done nothing when she started out on I’d Do Anything on the BBC,” he said. Barks reached the final of the 2008 talent show, which invited the public to choose an unknown actress to play Nancy in a new production of Lionel Bart’s Oliver! She finished third behind winner Jodie Prenger, but ultimately secured the coveted role in 2011 — a breakthrough that has now led to her biggest screen opportunity yet. Filming is now underway.

Wales begin their Six Nations campaign with an away fixture against Ireland in Dublin on Sunday, 7 February.

Ospreys will also be without back-row Tyler Ardron for approximately eight weeks after the Canada international underwent knee surgery in October, following an injury picked up at the World Cup. The dual absence is a significant blow for the region as they navigate a crucial phase of the season.

Chris Towers, Ospreys’ medical performance manager, said Webb’s rehabilitation is progressing well but emphasized the need to reach the right physical standards before a return. “His recovery is going well and we’re now concentrating on getting him to the physical level he needs to be in order to perform as we want,” Towers said. “He has begun running again, started doing some skills work, and the focus is on getting him available for selection at the end of February, which would be five months post-op.”

Webb, capped 16 times by Wales, recently renewed his national dual contract with Ospreys and the Welsh Rugby Union, turning down offers from elsewhere to remain with the region where he made his debut in 2007.

text:
President Donald Trump has expressed strong support for his senior adviser and son-in-law Jared Kushner amid reports that Kushner discussed establishing a secret communications channel with Russia’s ambassador during the presidential transition. In a statement to the New York Times, Mr Trump praised Kushner’s performance and character but did not directly address the specific allegations that have intensified scrutiny around the aide’s contacts with Moscow.

The New York Times and The Washington Post reported that Kushner sought to use Russian diplomatic facilities to conduct conversations beyond the reach of U.S. monitoring in December, weeks before Mr Trump took office. At the time, Kushner, who is married to the president’s eldest daughter, Ivanka Trump, was a private citizen. The reports emerged as Kushner was said to be under scrutiny in the FBI’s investigation into alleged Russian interference in the 2016 election. U.S. media outlets have cited officials saying investigators believe Kushner possesses information relevant to the probe, though he is not necessarily suspected of wrongdoing.

“Jared is doing a great job for the country. I have total confidence in him,” Mr Trump said in his statement. “He is respected by virtually everyone and is working on programs that will save our country billions of dollars. In addition to that, and perhaps more importantly, he is a very good person.”

Senior administration officials moved to downplay the significance of the allegations without confirming their accuracy. Homeland Security Secretary John Kelly told ABC News on Sunday that establishing back channels with foreign governments is “normal” and “acceptable.” He said such communications can be beneficial, especially with entities “not particularly friendly to us,” provided the information is shared within the government.

National Security Adviser H.R. McMaster echoed that sentiment, saying generally that the United States maintains back-channel communication with a number of countries. Neither official directly addressed the reported use of Russian facilities to avoid U.S. surveillance or the specific timing of Kushner’s contacts.

The president’s remarks came as he reportedly met with attorneys at the White House on Sunday, a sign of the growing legal focus on the Russia matter inside the administration. Mr Trump also took to Twitter to condemn what he described as fabricated leaks and anonymous sourcing, accusing the “fake news media” of making up stories. “Whenever you see the words ‘sources say’ in the fake news media, and they don’t mention names it is very possible that those sources don’t exist,” he wrote, declaring “#FakeNews is the enemy!”

The reports about Kushner add to a series of revelations about contacts between Trump associates and Russian officials that have fueled questions about the campaign’s interactions with Moscow and the conduct of the transition. The ongoing FBI inquiry remains a central challenge for the White House as it seeks to advance its agenda while confronting mounting scrutiny over Russia-related issues.

text:
Standard Chartered will cut up to a quarter of its senior managers as chief executive Bill Winters pushes through a sweeping cost reduction and restructuring after years of rapid expansion across its footprint. In a memo to staff, Winters said roles at director level and above will be reduced, leaving the bank with up to 25% fewer senior staff. About 4,000 bankers are in the grades affected. The lender employs roughly 88,000 people worldwide, up from around 44,000 in 2005, and sources told the BBC that some positions created during its post-crisis growth are no longer needed.

The bank said it had previously disclosed that further personnel changes were coming and that it had already moved to reduce management layers. Winters, who took over from former chief executive Peter Sands in June, has pledged to simplify Standard Chartered with a new leadership team and a simpler organisational structure.

In recent months the group has shed businesses in Hong Kong, China and Korea, booking a $219m gain and strengthening its capital position. It has also hired Mark Smith from Asia-focused rival HSBC as chief risk officer.

Winters has cut the dividend to help shore up the bank’s capital base, a buffer against unexpected financial shocks, and has not ruled out raising additional capital if needed. The measures aim to streamline operations and restore performance at the emerging-markets-focused lender.

text:
Ben Youngs says a renewed sense of freedom and belief under England head coach Eddie Jones and Leicester Tigers boss Aaron Mauger has helped him rediscover his best form. The 26-year-old scrum-half played a key role in England’s Six Nations Grand Slam, and as Leicester prepare for Sunday’s Champions Cup quarter-final against Stade Francais at Welford Road, Youngs told BBC Radio 5 live he feels invigorated on both fronts. “With Mauge and Eddie, I feel I can play like I did when I first came on the scene for Leicester, when I didn’t fear what might happen if it went wrong,” he said.

“It’s a new lease of life — I’ve been given confidence by both coaches to express myself,” Youngs added. “It’s given me a new motivation, and I feel I’m being challenged and tested every day.” Following England’s group-stage exit at last year’s World Cup, the 57-cap international was one of several senior players whose places came under scrutiny. Youngs, who toured with the British and Irish Lions in 2013, admitted he needed to convince Jones of his worth. “To start with he was probably testing me out a little bit,” he said. “But I feel like I’ve got a very good relationship with Eddie. He instils a huge amount of belief both within the squad and individually, and I really enjoy being coached by him.”

Youngs featured in all five of England’s Six Nations matches but began the Grand Slam decider against France in Paris on the bench, with Danny Care preferred to start. His second-half impact proved telling. “When [Jones] told me [I wasn’t starting], he said I was going to come off the bench and win us the Grand Slam. I thought, ‘I quite like the sound of that!’” Youngs said. “At that point I said to Eddie it’s just about winning the Grand Slam. Of course I want to start every game, but so does Danny, so that naturally isn’t going to happen. I was just happy that I could come on and really help the team. The plan paid off, so credit to him.”

At club level, Youngs believes his decision to recently sign a new contract with Leicester has already been vindicated. “Definitely,” he said. “I really think whatever happens this year, I feel like we are only just touching the surface under Mauge. Next season we have Matt Toomua coming in, JP Pietersen coming in. The best is yet to come.”

Listen to live commentary of Leicester Tigers versus Stade Francais on BBC Radio 5 live on Sunday at 13:45.

text:
Prof Calvin Jones has cautioned that expectations around the South Wales Metro risk outpacing reality, warning that the first tangible benefits may be felt in Cardiff before reaching the valleys. The Welsh Government continues to describe the Metro as “transformational” and hopes first services will be running by 2023, but Jones, of Cardiff Business School, told BBC’s Sunday Politics Wales the project is a minimum 15- to 20-year endeavour and will develop incrementally rather than delivering instant, sweeping change.

A remarkable glimpse of Britain’s prehistoric past has emerged off the Norfolk coast, where divers have uncovered a newly exposed section of a submerged forest believed to be part of Doggerland, the ancient land bridge that once connected Great Britain to continental Europe after the last Ice Age. Dawn Watson and Rob Spray, volunteer divers with the marine conservation project Seasearch, made the discovery about 30 metres (100 feet) offshore from Cley at a depth of around 9 metres (30 feet).

The forest was first revealed when thousands of tonnes of sand shifted during the powerful 2013 storm surge, peeling back layers that had long concealed ancient tree remains on the seabed. Watson initially found the submerged forest bed last year, describing to BBC Inside Out how they had come across “an enormous wave of black stuff,” which she later realised were the flattened remains of an oak woodland. On a subsequent visit, the pair located a Victorian anchor lying atop the ancient bed. During their latest dive, they found a newly uncovered stretch nearby.

“They say there’s a veneer of sand down there, but the word ‘veneer’ really doesn’t do it justice,” said Spray. “We dived and came across an area where it looked as if the sea bed was black. If you had a big broom it looked as if you could have swept it away, to reveal a flat black floor under thick sand. You get the impression it might stretch for tens of metres, but you could only see for five to six metres anyway. It was a lovely surprise but it’s very hard to get a complete scope or handle on it.”

Watson said the fresh exposure had rapidly attracted marine life. “Thousands of sea animals had swarmed in on it, creating excellent photographic opportunities,” she said. The divers noted that they approached the site from an unusual angle and could easily have missed the subtle transition where the sand layer thins to reveal the dark substrate beneath. “We really would have assumed that it would have been covered over again,” Spray added.

The pair hope to continue surveying the area with further dives to better understand the extent and condition of the prehistoric forest bed. “We’ll continue to survey the prehistoric forest bed but, as amateurs, resources are always limited,” Spray said. “But it’s a fine example of how citizen scientists often lead the way where ever-shrinking government resources may never reach.”

Doggerland’s inhabitants are thought to have endured centuries of rising seas before abandoning the low-lying landscape. The remaining communities were ultimately wiped out by a catastrophic five-metre tsunami around 8,200 years ago, leaving remnants of their environment preserved beneath the North Sea’s shifting sands.

Calls to protect Irish Sea habitats intensify as fishermen warn of economic pain

Conservationists and fishermen are at odds over whether two ecologically rich areas in the Irish Sea should be granted marine conservation zone (MCZ) status, amid a government review that could reshape protections and livelihoods. The Wildlife Trust has urged the UK government to designate Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg—located midway between Northern Ireland and the Isle of Man—as protected zones, warning that excluding them puts vulnerable sea life at risk. The Northern Ireland Fish Producers’ Association counters that the proposed sites are prime fishing grounds and that stricter rules would harm an industry that supports coastal communities.

In January, the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra), which has responsibility for the two offshore sites, did not include Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg among dedicated MCZs, arguing protection could have a “significant impact on Northern Ireland’s fishing sector.” The department plans to review that decision in the coming months as part of a wider consultation on new marine protections. Of nine MCZs proposed for the Irish Sea, two—Fylde and Cumbria Coast, off England—have already been approved.

MCZ status can restrict destructive activities such as dredging and trawling, measures proponents say are crucial to restoring habitats and safeguarding species. The Wildlife Trust highlights the presence of Dublin Bay prawns (nephrops) and ocean quahogs—long-lived clams that can survive for more than 500 years—as evidence of the sites’ ecological value. Emily Baxter, of the trust, said fisheries should recognise that well-managed MCZs can benefit both nature and the industry. “We’re not saying they would be banned outright from fishing in marine conservation zones,” she said. “But if we do want to conserve the special species, then it would make sense to restrict access. Supporting sustainable fisheries, instead of encouraging overfishing and habitat destruction, would increase fish landings, generate more income and create more jobs in the sector. If these areas are allowed to recover, there will be more of them (nephrops) and they can grow bigger.”

Dick James, head of the Northern Ireland Fish Producers’ Association, warned that designating Slieve na Griddle and South Rigg would cause real hardship. “Eight thousand tonnes of nephrops are trawled from the Irish Sea each year; it’s a £20m industry,” he said. “We’ve offered alternatives which don’t leave us entirely clear of the issue, but the areas they’ve picked are the most intensely fished areas in the Irish Sea. In some of the areas we’ve put forward, the fisheries are not as intense. We’re basically hoping that common sense will prevail and that there are alternatives, more diverse than the areas they’ve proposed in the first instance.”

The push for new protections comes amid a decade-long effort to expand marine conservation across UK waters. In 2013, 127 zones were initially proposed following two years of negotiations among fishermen, conservationists and other sea users. To date, 27 have been designated, and the government is seeking public views on a further 23. The consultation is due to close on 24 April.

In his 1989 statement, Kirton said: “Chief Superintendent Duckenfield told us the gate had been forced and an in-rush of Liverpool supporters had caused casualties.” Reports suggesting fans had broken in were widely carried by the media for much of the day, the inquests heard, until a press conference on the evening of the disaster. Jurors were told that South Yorkshire Police’s chief constable, Peter Wright, later told journalists that “a gate had been opened by police.”

Kirton told the jury that it was not until the evening press conference that “it became apparent” a gate had not been forced, though he was earlier aware that some fans believed the gate had been opened by the police.

He also recounted a discussion with Mr Mackrell at about 14:40 GMT regarding the possibility of delaying kick-off, saying Mackrell told him there were still many fans outside—his recollection was “around 20,000,” a figure he found high for that time. Uber is facing a landmark legal challenge in the UK over the employment status and working conditions of its drivers, brought by law firm Leigh Day on behalf of the GMB union. The case argues that Uber does not currently ensure its drivers are paid at least the minimum wage or receive paid holiday, and that the company denies drivers rights normally afforded to employees by classifying them as “partners.”

Uber operates a car hire smartphone app that connects passengers to drivers and covers London and more than 300 cities worldwide. Using the app, passengers can request to be picked up from any location within those areas. Passengers pay Uber for the journey, and the company then passes on a percentage of that payment to the driver.

Leigh Day’s lawyers claim that Uber’s contract terms breach UK employment law and that the firm’s practices raise serious health and safety concerns. They allege Uber does not ensure its drivers take rest breaks or adhere to a maximum number of hours per week. The lawyers argue this creates a substantial risk to all road users, particularly given that, according to Uber’s chief executive, there will be 42,000 Uber drivers in London in 2016.

The law firm added there had been reports of drivers being suspended or deactivated by Uber after making complaints about unlawful treatment, without being given any opportunity to challenge the claims. Leigh Day says the law requires that workers should not be denied the right to work for raising such issues, and that any retaliation for bringing concerns forward would be unlawful.

If successful, the legal action could result in substantial payouts for drivers, including compensation for past failures by the company to make appropriate payments to what the lawyers argue are Uber’s workers. Nigel Mackay, a lawyer in the employment team at Leigh Day, said: “Uber not only pays the drivers but it also effectively controls how much passengers are charged and requires drivers to follow particular routes. As well as this, it uses a ratings system to assess drivers’ performance. We believe that it’s clear from the way Uber operates that it owes the same responsibilities towards its drivers as any other employer does to its workers. In particular, its drivers should not be denied the right to minimum wage and paid leave.”

The case is the first of its kind to be brought against the San Francisco-based firm in the UK, although Uber has faced legal action elsewhere around the world. Last week, taxi drivers in Toronto, Canada’s largest city, initiated legal proceedings against Uber. It operates 18 shows worldwide, a mix of touring productions and long-running residencies in Las Vegas, and generates roughly $1 billion (£600 million) in annual revenue. The food and drug safety branch of Huzhou police warned that chronic exposure to high aluminium levels could damage bones and nerves and impair memory, advising pregnant women, children and older adults to avoid consuming any suspect jellyfish products. With more than 70% of ballots counted, officials reported that 99.8% supported the holiday. About 1.2 million people were eligible to vote, and turnout was put at more than 56%.

The Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina, based in Sarajevo, had ruled that celebrating 9 January as a public holiday in Republika Srpska discriminates against Muslim Bosniaks and Catholic Croats and ordered the date to be changed. The 9 January date is deeply contentious. It marks the day in 1992 when Bosnian Serb leaders declared the creation of their own state within Bosnia, a step that helped ignite a war in which around 100,000 people were killed. It also coincides with an Orthodox Christian religious holiday, underscoring the court’s finding that it marginalizes non-Serbs.

International High Representative Valentin Inzko condemned the referendum, telling the BBC it was “illegal and unconstitutional,” and stressing that Constitutional Court decisions are “final and binding.” The Office of the High Representative retains powers under the 1995 Dayton Peace Agreement to remove officials who threaten the accord, though such measures have been used rarely in recent years.

Digital connectivity is set for a significant test in the Scottish Borders this weekend as organisers of the Tweedlove Bike Festival trial “TV white space” technology in Glentress Forest to power live streaming and on-site internet access for spectators and competitors. These gaps vary by region but can be harnessed by specially configured devices to carry data over longer distances and through obstacles that typically disrupt conventional signals. Microsoft’s Jim Beveridge, senior director of international technology policy, highlighted the versatility already demonstrated by white space pilots. “We’ve successfully trialled it in everything from lifeboats to businesses and now in sport,” he said. “It brings people together in a way that just wasn’t possible five years ago and it just might bring some of the superstars here this weekend direct to your mobile.”

An invasive garden pest is rapidly spreading across south-east England, displacing slugs and snails for the first time in nearly a decade at the top of the Royal Horticultural Society’s most-unwanted list. The box tree caterpillar, the larval stage of the moth Diaphania perspectalis, was first detected in UK private gardens in 2011 after adult moths were reported in 2008. Since then, it has moved beyond its initial London stronghold, alarming gardeners and heritage institutions that rely on box (Buxus) to shape formal garden designs.

The RHS says enquiries to its entomology team in 2015 reflect the surge in concern: the box tree caterpillar accounted for 433 queries, or 17% of all pest-related enquiries, placing it at number one. Slugs and snails, the perennial scourge of beds and borders, fell to second with 122 enquiries. Experts warn the “invasive bug” could continue to spread more widely in the UK if not actively managed.

Native to Asia and believed to have originated in China, the moth is thought to have reached Britain either by flying across the English Channel or by hitching a ride among imported plants. Once established, it can devastate box plants. Females lay overlapping sheets of pale yellow eggs on the undersides of leaves. After hatching, the green-and-black striped larvae feed within protective webbing, spinning silken structures around leaves and twigs to conceal themselves. As they grow to around 4cm long, caterpillars can completely defoliate box shrubs, leaving brown, skeletonised foliage and weakened plants.

The RHS advises several control measures, including physically removing caterpillars by hand where feasible, or deploying biological controls and approved insecticides to reduce populations. Early detection and regular inspection of box hedges and topiary are critical to limiting damage.

Experts stress that the caterpillar is unrelated to box blight, a fungal disease that causes bare patches and dieback, where leaves die back from their tips. Nonetheless, 2025 has been challenging for box plants overall, with box blight among the most frequently reported garden diseases. High spring temperatures combined with rainfall created ideal conditions for fungal spread, leading to a spike in enquiries. The warmest, wettest December on record further fuelled unexpected disease activity that is normally suppressed by colder weather.

Because box plants underpin the structure of many historic formal gardens, both the caterpillar and box blight pose a serious risk to the UK’s horticultural heritage. Dunkirk Veterans Return to Allied Beach Memorial for 75th Anniversary of Operation Dynamo

Seven veterans of Operation Dynamo gathered at the Allied Beach Memorial in Dunkirk to pay their respects during a poignant service marking the 75th anniversary of the mass evacuation. Arthur Taylor, 94, described feeling “enormous tears” as he laid a wreath, flanked by his military grandsons, in a ceremony that brought together veterans, families, and dignitaries to honor one of World War Two’s defining moments.

Operation Dynamo, staged between 26 May and 4 June 1940, saw hundreds of vessels—naval ships, merchant craft, and civilian “little ships”—rescue 338,000 Allied troops from the beaches of northern France after they retreated before advancing Nazi forces. Though hailed as a triumph of courage and coordination, the operation also carried a heavy toll, with about 90,000 left dead, wounded, or taken prisoner. Historians regard the feat as a pivotal turning point that helped sustain Britain’s war effort.

Under grey skies, a crowd of onlookers gathered in the memorial square to witness the service. Wrapped against the cold, the veterans listened as the French army performed music, followed by schoolchildren reading aloud a newspaper account written in the days immediately after the evacuation. The intergenerational tribute set a reflective tone for the ceremony.

Wreaths were laid at the foot of the memorial wall by French and British dignitaries, including Prince Michael of Kent, honorary admiral of the Association of Dunkirk Little Ships. Applause broke out spontaneously as Mr. Taylor stepped forward to place his wreath on behalf of the Bournemouth branch of the Dunkirk Veterans’ Association, supported by his grandsons—Royal Marines Major Stuart Taylor, 41, and Warrant Officer Second Class Ian Taylor, 39, of the Royal Electrical and Mechanical Engineers.

“I appreciated them all clapping. I didn’t expect it,” Mr. Taylor said afterward, admitting to “enormous tears” during the tribute. Major Taylor called it a “real honor” to be present for the service and described the moment as “very proud” for the family. As God Save the Queen rang out, those veterans able to stand saluted before making the short journey down to the beach.

The commemorations began on Thursday as around 50 “little ships” that participated in the 1940 rescue crossed from Kent to Dunkirk. On Friday, a handful of veterans gathered at the British Memorial in the Dunkirk Military Cemetery for another remembrance service. Leading that ceremony, Royal Navy chaplain Gordon Warren offered a solemn reflection: “Whilst we thank God this weekend for those wartime miracles during the evacuation, let us never forget the precious souls who are commemorated here and who never came back. We will remember them.”

Observances continue on Sunday with the unveiling of a memorial plaque at the site of the MV Crested Eagle, a paddle steamer sunk with 300 soldiers aboard, and a commemorative service for the Association of Dunkirk Little Ships on the quayside. Together, the events underscore the enduring legacy of Operation Dynamo and the bond between generations united by memory and sacrifice.

The fare system allows bus passengers to make an extra journey within an hour of touching in when using an Oyster card or contactless payment. Previously, customers were obliged to pay £1.50 each time they boarded a bus. The hopper-fare will “help ensure everyone will be able to afford to travel around the city,” Mayor Sadiq Khan said, confirming the policy is scheduled to be introduced in September.

Unveiling his first major transport measure since taking office, Mr Khan framed the change as both personal and practical. “My dad drove the number 44 bus and transport in London has always been a big part of my life,” he said. “The cost of a fare in London has risen for eight years in a row and now that I’m mayor I am determined to prevent the cost of travel from becoming a barrier to work.” Under his predecessor Boris Johnson, bus fares rose in successive years, a trend Khan says he is keen to reverse or mitigate.

Under the new hopper-fare, a single bus journey will still cost £1.50, but passengers will be able to board a second bus within 60 minutes of their first tap without paying again. The change applies to Oyster and contactless payments; London buses stopped accepting cash in 2014, and riders today either purchase single tickets or use travelcards that cover multiple journeys in a day. Unlike the Tube, where prices are calculated by zones with automatic transfers via the same fare, bus passengers currently pay for every boarding, a disparity many have argued is unfair.

Transport for London (TfL) said it does not yet have the technology to allow unlimited bus transfers within a one-hour window but aims to upgrade its ticketing systems in 2017, with the possibility of introducing unlimited timed bus fares by the end of 2018. TfL has previously estimated a one-hour bus ticket would cost around £50 million a year. High Court backs government plan to close Independent Living Fund in June 2015

The High Court has upheld the government’s decision to close the Independent Living Fund (ILF), a £320m scheme that provides support to around 18,000 severely disabled people across the UK, ruling that ministers acted lawfully in planning to end the fund on 30 June 2015. Delivering her judgment, Mrs Justice Andrews expressed sympathy for those affected, acknowledging the closure would be a “great disappointment” for many, but concluded that the legal challenge did not establish that the decision breached equality duties.

The ILF, established to help disabled people live independently rather than in residential care, offers payments that many recipients use to employ personal assistants and access support tailored to individual needs. During an October hearing, David Wolfe QC, representing two severely disabled claimants in lead cases, argued that the Work and Pensions Secretary had unlawfully failed to discharge his public sector equality duty under the Equality Act 2010. He told the court the claimants receive between £450 and £500 per week from the ILF, funding he said was critical to enabling them to live in their own homes, work, and study.

The application for judicial review dismissed on Monday marked the second legal battle over the closure. In November 2013, the Court of Appeal overturned an earlier ruling from April 2013 that had found the government’s original decision to be lawful. Following that setback, ministers announced a fresh decision to close the fund, underpinned by new equalities analysis prepared by the Department for Work and Pensions, which was subsequently challenged again in court.

The government argues that reforms to social care have called into question the need for a separate funding stream, asserting that the vast majority of disabled people with care needs are already supported through the adult social care system administered by local authorities. Under the plan to close the ILF, funding is to be transferred to councils.

However, disability rights advocates have warned of serious consequences. The charity Scope said disabled people could be left without enough support, with chief executive Richard Hawkes describing the care system as “on its knees.” He cautioned that closure is “likely to lead to fewer disabled people being able to live independently,” adding: “Funding will be transferred to councils, but there will be no guarantee that the money will be used to support disabled people to live independently, or that former ILF users will receive the same levels of support, given the pressures on local authority finances.”

Wheelchair user John Kelly, 45, from Wimbledon, who attended the ruling, called the decision “bonkers.” “I am absolutely gutted — not just for myself but for the thousands of people this decision will impact on,” he said.

The Equality and Human Rights Commission has previously warned that closing the ILF would “result in loss of dignity and independence for many ILF recipients,” and could put the UK at risk of breaching international commitments to support disabled people.

World Bank Urges Criminal Justice Crackdown on Illegal Logging

Most illegal logging operations are controlled by organized crime and channel profits to corrupt officials, the World Bank warns in a new report calling for a tougher criminal justice response to protect forests and communities. The study, titled Justice for Forests, identifies Indonesia, Madagascar and several West African nations among those heavily affected, and says targeted prosecutions and stronger law enforcement capacity can deliver swift, measurable impact.

“We need to fight organised crime in illegal logging the way we go after gangsters selling drugs or racketeering,” said Jean Pesme, manager of the World Bank Financial Market Integrity team. The report argues that the illegal timber trade mirrors other prohibited commodities, with sophisticated networks laundering wood, bribing officials, falsifying documentation and exploiting weak governance. Analysts estimate that an area of forest the size of a soccer pitch is illegally logged every second.

Despite the scale, most forest crimes go undetected, unreported or ignored, the report says. Investigations, when they occur, are often “amateurish and inconclusive,” and prosecutions too frequently target minor players driven by poverty while leaving higher-level profiteers untouched. Illegal logging ranges from mechanized crews stripping vast tracts to individual villagers gathering fuelwood, underscoring the need for responses that distinguish between subsistence and organized criminal activity.

Some countries are beginning to turn the tide. Indonesia and Papua New Guinea are moving to strengthen enforcement and bring cases against figures higher up the criminal food chain. The World Bank urges aid donors to support programs that build the capacity of law enforcement agencies, prosecutors and courts to pursue complex timber crime, including financial investigations that trace profits and expose corruption.

Western governments, consumers and businesses have a key role in cutting off demand for illicit wood. The United States strengthened the Lacey Act three years ago, making companies liable for ensuring that wood sold in the US comes from legal sources. Several firms have faced scrutiny under the amendment, including the iconic Gibson guitar company. The European Union has introduced similar due diligence requirements, and a growing number of buyers now insist on timber that is demonstrably legal and sustainably harvested.

A 2010 study by the London-based Chatham House think-tank found that such measures had reduced illegal logging by about a quarter over the previous eight years. It urged Japan, a major timber consumer, to enact its own legislation. With Chinese consumption rising rapidly, campaigners are increasingly focusing on Beijing. Two years ago, the Environmental Investigation Agency reported beds made from illegally sourced Madagascan rosewood selling in the Chinese capital for up to $1 million, illustrating both the profits at stake and the urgency of closing global loopholes.

Authorities said up to 10,000 mourners will be permitted inside each day, as Thailand begins a long, formal farewell to the monarch who reigned for seven decades and was revered across the nation.

In older times, the king’s remains would have been interred in the urn. King Bhumibol requested that his body be placed in a coffin instead, which is concealed behind the ceremonial vessel. Margaret Thatcher’s premiership left an indelible mark on Scotland, reshaping its economy, politics and public life in ways still debated today. Supporters argue she confronted a failing system with uncompromising clarity; critics say her policies brought lasting social damage and fueled a new Scottish political consciousness.

Former Scottish Secretary Lord Lang recalls a country already in deep trouble when she arrived in Downing Street. “All she was doing was clearing away the debris of what was already a desert on a life support machine,” he says. “The life support machine was one fed by taxation pumped in by the Westminster government.” State-supported heavy industry, long central to many Scottish communities, was left to decline. British Steel’s mill at Gartcosh, the Invergordon aluminium smelter and the Corpach pulp mill were among the casualties of a new economic approach that favored market discipline over public subsidy.

The most dramatic confrontation came with the miners’ strike, a year-long dispute that became a defining battle of the 1980s. Thatcher famously labeled striking miners “the enemy within,” a phrase that crystallized both her resolve and her polarizing effect. “Miners were proud people. Proud to work in the industry and she took that from us, her and her government, during that period,” says Nicky Wilson of the National Union of Mineworkers. “I personally don’t think anybody involved in that time will ever forgive her.”

Yet one policy proved widely popular across Scotland: the sale of council houses. Even where her party struggled at the ballot box, tenants embraced the opportunity to buy their homes, transforming the housing landscape and wealth ownership for many families.

Thatcher articulated the moral case for her economics in her “Sermon on the Mound,” addressing the Church of Scotland’s General Assembly in May 1988. “It is not the creation of wealth that is wrong but the love of money for its own sake,” she told the Kirk, seeking to align enterprise with ethical purpose.

Another flashpoint was the Community Charge—better known as the Poll Tax—introduced in Scotland first. The flat-rate levy, applied equally to rich and poor, ignited anger, street protests and widespread non-payment. Former Labour MP and MSP Dennis Canavan argues the policy galvanized demands for devolution. “This was such a blatant injustice—this Poll Tax—that people then began to see that this could never happen if we had a Scottish Parliament.”

The tax proved untenable in England too, hastening Thatcher’s downfall and rebellion within her own party. Former Scottish Secretary Malcolm Rifkind says her style grated: “She was a bossy English woman. They could probably have put up with one or even two of these but all three simultaneously was a bit too much.”

Her legacy, says SNP leader and First Minister Alex Salmond, is etched into the concrete of Holyrood. “What Margaret Thatcher did was turn the Scottish Parliament from being a nice idea—democratic advance—to being something absolutely essential.” To many, her strengths were her weaknesses: tough, decisive, and, critics insist, inflexible—qualities that defined the Iron Lady and a transformative, contested era.

text:
Because today's Budget is massively less austere than the one forged with them in March, just before the election

The chancellor’s latest Budget represents a notable softening of austerity compared with plans outlined before the general election. By the end of the parliament, George Osborne now intends to reduce spending on public services by just under £18bn a year—still significant, but less than half the £42bn in annual cuts previously proposed for 2018-19. As a result, the scale of retrenchment is no longer widely viewed by economists and politicians as ideologically driven or implausible.

The lesser squeeze is financed in large part by tax rises that collectively outweigh headline-grabbing giveaways. According to the Office for Budget Responsibility (OBR), the measures will raise £47bn over five years. Key components include reform of dividend taxation, expected to yield around £2bn annually, and a rise in insurance premium tax projected to bring in £1.5bn per year. Against these increases stand around £25bn in tax cuts, most visibly through higher personal allowances and an increase in the threshold for the 40% income-tax band, alongside a two percentage point reduction in the main rate of corporation tax. With a pledged corporation tax rate of 18%, Britain could start to look to some multinationals like a near-tax haven, intensifying competitive pressures on other jurisdictions.

Welfare and social security are still slated for deep reductions, albeit more slowly than first advertised. The £12bn of cuts will be phased over four years rather than two, spreading the impact though not diminishing its severity. Millions are expected to feel the strain, particularly middle-income families, who will absorb much of the effect of tax-credit reforms forecast to raise around £4.5bn each year. In a striking departure for a Conservative administration that espouses market solutions, the Budget also creates a new official living wage—effectively an intervention to set the price of labour above the current minimum wage. Critics liken the move to 1970s-style Labour price-setting, noting the tension it introduces for businesses facing higher staffing costs.

Osborne’s timetable for restoring the public finances has slipped. The surplus he said would arrive in 2018-19 is now forecast for 2019-20. The OBR estimates the national debt will be £18bn higher by 2020 than promised in March, with £3.5bn of that directly attributable to decisions announced today. In short, the chancellor’s effort to “mend the roof while the sun is shining,” to use his preferred phrase, is proceeding more slowly than previously pledged—even as the Budget’s mix of tax rises, targeted reliefs, and phased welfare cuts reshapes the UK’s fiscal landscape.

Government proposes new limits and oversight for pre-charge police bail

Theresa May has unveiled plans to overhaul pre-charge police bail in England and Wales, introducing time limits and new oversight requirements amid mounting concern over suspects being kept on bail for extended periods without charge.

Under the proposals, a senior police officer would have to authorise any bail period beyond 28 days, and a magistrate would be required to approve extensions beyond three months. At present, there is no statutory time limit on pre-charge bail and no requirement for police to seek external approval to extend it.

Mrs May said the reforms would be taken forward in the next Parliament, describing it as “simply not acceptable” that pre-charge bail could last “months or years.” She also announced a “new presumption” in favour of releasing suspects without bail, with conditions to be imposed “only where it is necessary or proportionate,” in a bid to drive down what she called the “inappropriate use” of bail.

The Home Office said the revised approach reflects feedback on earlier proposals that would have required court approval after 28 days. Under the new plan, a superintendent could authorise an extension at 28 days, but only in exceptional circumstances and up to a total of three months. Any further extension beyond three months would need to be sanctioned by a magistrate.

Mrs May added that some elements, including issuing national guidance and collecting data on the use of police bail, would not require legislation and could begin immediately.

The Association of Chief Police Officers (Acpo) said pre-charge bail remained “an essential tool in securing justice,” but agreed the system should be “efficient and proportionate” for both victims and suspects. “Each and every investigation follows a different path. Less than 2% of arrests result in a person being on bail for more than six months. However, in an increasingly globalised and digitised world some cases are complex… and cannot be rushed,” an Acpo spokesman said.

Calls for reform have intensified following high-profile cases. Earlier this month, broadcaster Paul Gambaccini urged MPs to impose limits on pre-charge bail, recounting how officers and prosecutors “sat” on his case for 12 months before informing him he would not be charged over an allegation of historical sexual abuse.

The government’s proposals will be subject to parliamentary scrutiny in the next legislative session.

Australia will tighten the assets test for the age pension, boosting payments for retirees with modest holdings while reducing or removing benefits for wealthier homeowners, as the government seeks savings ahead of the 12 May budget. Social Services Minister Scott Morrison said the overhaul would save about A$2.4bn (US$2bn; £1.3bn) a year and better target support. “We want the welfare system to be focused on those in greatest need and in the pension system, that’s those with low or modest assets,” he told the ABC. Under the changes, the government estimates roughly 172,000 pensioners will be A$30 a fortnight better off. About 91,000 retirees who own their homes and have other assets worth more than A$823,000 would lose access to the part-pension.

The package replaces the government’s earlier, highly contested plan to alter pension indexation by tying increases to inflation rather than wages. Seniors’ groups argued that linking to inflation would have left pensioners worse off over time because prices were rising more slowly than average earnings. The government has now scrapped that proposal, keeping the existing wage-based indexation.

Advocacy groups broadly welcomed the pivot to the assets test. Combined Pensioners and Superannuants’ Association spokesperson Amelia Christie said tightening the test was “definitely fairer” than cutting indexation. “Tightening the pension asset test makes more sense both from a financial and fairness perspective if you compare it with the 2014 budget proposal to cut pension indexation and reduce the value of the pension over time,” she said.

However, Christie noted the changes still conflict with the government’s pre-election pledge not to touch pensions. She urged ministers to focus instead on superannuation tax concessions, which she said overwhelmingly benefit high-income earners. “This lost revenue should be tackled before pensioners face a hit to their incomes,” she said.

Education Secretary John Swinney has made it clear he expects the group to challenge him on policy and delivery. The panel was set up after last year's Holyrood elections. It includes members from Australia, the US, Canada, Norway, Sweden, Finland, Malaysia and the UK.

Recommendations from the group are contained in a short report produced by the Scottish Government’s International Council of Education Advisers following its most recent meeting in Edinburgh in February. The council’s role is to generate ideas for improvement and provide robust challenge to ministers as reforms are taken forward.

The report warns that one of the core aims of Curriculum for Excellence (CfE) risks being diluted by the way plans to drive up performance are implemented. CfE was designed to focus on the “whole child”, ensuring education supports young people to become successful learners, confident individuals, effective contributors and responsible citizens, rather than concentrating solely on academic outcomes. In parallel, the National Improvement Framework (NIF) has been established to raise attainment, with key goals including improving literacy and numeracy and closing the gap between the most and least disadvantaged pupils.

While the council said CfE and NIF share a clear and positive narrative, it expressed concern that system pressures could push schools away from the whole-child approach toward a narrower focus on what is easier to measure. It highlighted three priority areas, and noted evidence of collaborative intent across the system, but concluded that collaboration remains uneven and insufficiently embedded in practice.

The advisors also cautioned against an overemphasis on structural changes. They argued that culture and capacity are, arguably, more important drivers of improvement than reorganising governance or management arrangements. The Scottish Government recently announced plans to give head teachers more formal powers in an effort to accelerate school-level decision making. Some members of the panel had previously told BBC Scotland that changing structures alone would not deliver better outcomes.

A Scottish government spokeswoman said: “We value the council’s expertise, robust challenge and input into our policy thinking, and our decision to further empower schools and teachers took their advice into account alongside other evidence.”

Mr Swinney has encouraged the council to test and challenge the government’s approach as reforms are developed and implemented. A formal report on the actions required by the Scottish Government to deliver its vision for education is expected to be produced by the advisors next year, building on the initial findings from the February meeting and setting out detailed recommendations for policy and delivery.

UCU to ballot for industrial action as university redundancy dispute escalates

The University and College Union (UCU) has announced a ballot for industrial action after what it says were serious breaches of agreed procedures in a growing dispute over job cuts. The union claims more than 250 staff now fear for their jobs, while the university insists no one faces compulsory redundancy and has offered further talks.

“We now feel we have no alternative but to ballot for industrial action,” said UCU regional official Martyn Moss. “Out of the blue, 37 people who thought they were safely on the books of the university suddenly faced a redundancy process… to make it worse, another 219 staff are also at risk of losing their jobs.”

The dispute began in April when 37 staff who had been on the university’s redeployment register for three months or more were told they could face redundancy. The union says the move marked a dramatic departure from the university’s long-standing policy of allowing staff to remain on the register until redeployed without fear of redundancy. It alleges managers rode roughshod over procedures while the redeployment policy was being revised and “simply went ahead and issued 37 ‘at risk of redundancy’ notices.”

Tensions escalated in July when 219 employees in the computer support and maintenance team were informed the university planned to cut 68 posts. The university disputes the union’s characterization, saying no compulsory redundancies are planned and that letters sent to staff were requests for volunteers. A university spokesman said management had offered “further discussions to try to resolve any issues.”

Formal talks broke down last month. UCU members have until 20 November to vote on industrial action. Both sides say they remain committed to further discussions, potentially with the assistance of the arbitration service Acas.

A local resident told Reuters that several thousand people had taken to the streets. Images shared by users on Weibo-like platforms showed flames engulfing vehicles and police cars overturned, while another purported local resident posted a photo of paramilitary police in riot gear deployed at the scene.

Authorities have pledged an investigation into Gan’s death and the events that followed. Regional Leaders Sign Peace Accord in Addis Ababa, Paving Path Toward Stability in Eastern DR Congo

A landmark peace agreement aimed at ending years of instability in eastern Democratic Republic of Congo (DR Congo) was signed in Addis Ababa in the presence of UN Secretary General Ban Ki-moon, who expressed hope the deal would usher in “an era of peace and stability” for the Great Lakes region. Leaders and representatives from 11 countries signed the accord, which could pave the way for a special UN intervention brigade to be deployed to eastern DR Congo alongside renewed political efforts to consolidate peace.

“As many as 800,000 people have been displaced since the March 23 (M23) rebel group took up arms against the Kinshasa government last May,” Mr Ban noted, cautioning that the agreement was “only the beginning of a comprehensive approach that will require sustained engagement.” An earlier attempt to secure signatures last month was called off at the last minute, underscoring the fragility of recent diplomatic efforts.

Heads of state and officials from Mozambique, Rwanda, Tanzania, South Africa, Democratic Republic of Congo, Congo Republic, and South Sudan attended the ceremony, reflecting the regional scope of the crisis and the shared interest in finding a lasting solution. The M23 movement says its campaign is driven by the need to improve living conditions in eastern DR Congo, but the United Nations has long alleged that the group is backed by Rwanda, whose security landscape has been intertwined with DR Congo’s since perpetrators of the 1994 genocide fled across the border.

Bosco Ntaganda, widely accused of being among the M23’s leaders, previously served as an officer in the Rwandan army before joining a DR Congo rebel movement. He is wanted by the International Criminal Court for allegedly using child soldiers, while the UN says he controls several mines in the country’s east. The group briefly seized Goma, the capital of North Kivu province, last November after carving out territory in the area.

Talks between DR Congo’s government and M23 representatives have been taking place in Uganda to address a range of issues. The rebels declared a unilateral ceasefire in January, though a previous effort collapsed in December after they accused President Joseph Kabila of failing to honour a deal to integrate fighters into the national army. For over 15 years, the region’s mineral wealth has been heavily exploited by multiple actors, with little investment in DR Congo’s infrastructure—an imbalance the new agreement seeks to help redress.

In a statement, Mr Skelton’s sister, Laura Skelton, said: “My heart is breaking right now for my brother. He was a kind and caring person. What happened was out of character. What a lovely person he was. Words can’t express the sadness we all feel, you didn’t deserve this.”

Neighbours described Mr Skelton as “mild mannered and polite.” Paul Mitten, who lived in the flat above him on Durham Street, said: “When I found out I just started crying because it just hit me for six knowing that what’s happened over there was the lad who lived under me. He was quiet, placid, looked after his animals. I can’t believe it. I can’t get over it. I’ve not been able to sleep. He’s always been polite to people, he’s always said ‘hi’ when he’s walked past… can’t say a bad word about him.”

Humberside Police said armed officers were deployed to the Holderness Road area at about 09:20 GMT following reports of a man carrying an axe, responding to calls from members of the public. “The area where we live now is pretty much like a ghost town and anybody who is there is wearing protective safety masks,” said Roy Keld, a mechanical engineer from Sedgefield who has lived in China for six years. “We’ve been warned if it rains to wear long-sleeved clothes, long trousers, that kind of thing, and use an umbrella. With the area densely populated, Keld said many displaced residents have taken shelter in schools and tents as authorities continue to clear the area and assess damage. “There’s a lot of people just living in schools at the moment, and tents. It’s a very densely populated area. So where do you put people?” he said.

The China Earthquake Networks Centre said the magnitude of the first blast was equivalent to detonating three tonnes of TNT, while the second was equivalent to 21 tonnes. Keld’s employer, UK-based Heat Tech Tooling, located about 25 miles (40km) from the blast site, has not been affected.
